nodes.title: Sets: Representation, Operations, Venn Diagrams
nodes.description: Sets are the language in which the rest of higher mathematics is written: collections of well-defined objects, described in roster or set-builder form. You will operate on sets with union, intersection, difference and complement, picture them with Venn diagrams, and use counting rules like n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A∩B). Mastering this vocabulary pays off immediately in relations, functions and probability.
learning_outcomes: Can write a set in roster and set-builder form and decide whether a collection is well-defined
Can distinguish element membership (∈) from subset inclusion (⊂) and list all subsets of a small set
Can compute union, intersection, difference and complement, and represent them on Venn diagrams
Can use n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A∩B) to solve survey-style counting problems
Can work with intervals of real numbers as sets and take complements within a universal set

misconceptions.description: Confuses 'is an element of' with 'is a subset of': writes {2} ∈ {1,2,3} or 2 ⊂ {1,2,3}.
misconceptions.signal: Uses ∈ and ⊂ interchangeably; says a single element 'is a subset' without braces, or that {2} is an element of {1,2,3}.
misconceptions.remedy: Use a box metaphor: elements are things inside the box, subsets are smaller boxes you could pack from those things. Drill contrast pairs like 2 ∈ A vs {2} ⊂ A vs {2} ∈ {{2},3} until the student verbalises the difference.

misconceptions.description: Thinks the empty set contains something, e.g. that ∅ = {0} or that ∅ ∈ every set because '∅ ⊂ every set'.
misconceptions.signal: Writes {0} for the empty set, or claims n(∅) = 1; mixes up ∅ ⊂ A (always true) with ∅ ∈ A (usually false).
misconceptions.remedy: Count subsets of small sets explicitly ({} has exactly 0 elements but IS a subset of everything). Contrast ∅, {0} and {∅} side by side and ask for n( ) of each.

misconceptions.description: Believes n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) always, forgetting to subtract the overlap.
misconceptions.signal: In survey problems, adds the two group sizes and gets more people than exist in the class.
misconceptions.remedy: Draw the Venn diagram and physically shade the intersection twice while adding, making the double count visible; then subtract it once. Re-solve the same problem numerically from the three disjoint regions.

misconceptions.description: Treats set difference as commutative: A − B = B − A.
misconceptions.signal: Computes B − A when asked for A − B, or claims the two are always equal.
misconceptions.remedy: Concrete counterexample with small sets ({1,2,3} − {2,3,4} = {1} but {2,3,4} − {1,2,3} = {4}); tie to the asymmetry of subtraction of numbers.

real_world_hooks: Students who play cricket vs football in your class — who plays both, who plays neither?
Streaming subscriptions: Netflix ∪ Hotstar users in a colony survey
Blood groups as a partition of a population
WhatsApp groups as sets of contacts: intersection = people in both groups
teaching.video_search: sets venn diagrams union intersection class 11

questions.prompt: Let A = {1, 2, 3}. Which of the following statements is TRUE?

options.diagnosis: Reverses the membership relation entirely; needs the 'object in a box' picture rebuilt from scratch.

questions.explanation: 2 is an object listed inside A, so 2 ∈ A. The subset symbol needs a set on the left: {2} ⊂ A is true, but 2 ⊂ A is not meaningful, and {2} is not one of the listed elements of A, so {2} ∈ A is false.

questions.prompt: In a class of 50 students, 30 like cricket, 25 like football, and 12 like both. How many students like at least one of the two sports?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted the overlap twice (30 + 25 − 12 − 12); over-corrected the double count.
Reported n(A∩B) instead of n(A∪B); confused 'both' with 'at least one'.

questions.explanation: n(C∪F) = n(C) + n(F) − n(C∩F) = 30 + 25 − 12 = 43. Adding 30 + 25 = 55 counts the 12 both-lovers twice — and even exceeds the class size of 50, a built-in sanity check.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is true for ALL sets A and B?

options.text: If A ⊂ B, then A ∪ B = B
n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) for all finite sets

questions.explanation: If every element of A is already in B, uniting them adds nothing new, so A ∪ B = B. The empty set is a SUBSET of every set (∅ ⊂ A) but rarely an element; set difference is not commutative; and the addition rule needs the correction term −n(A∩B) whenever the sets overlap.

nodes.title: Relations and Functions: Domain, Range, Standard Functions
nodes.description: A relation pairs elements of one set with another via the Cartesian product; a function is the special relation where every input gets exactly one output. You will find domains and ranges, and meet the standard function family — identity, constant, polynomial, rational, modulus, signum, greatest integer — with their graphs. Functions are the central objects of calculus, so fluency here directly powers limits and derivatives.
learning_outcomes: Can form Cartesian products and count/list relations from A to B
Can decide whether a given relation (as pairs, arrow diagram or graph) is a function, citing the definition
Can find the domain and range of algebraic functions involving fractions and square roots
Can sketch and read graphs of identity, constant, modulus, signum and greatest-integer functions
Can perform algebra of functions: sum, difference, product, quotient with correct domains

misconceptions.description: Believes every relation is a function; accepts an input having two different outputs.
misconceptions.signal: Calls {(1,a),(1,b)} a function; ignores the vertical line test on graphs like x = y².
misconceptions.remedy: Vending machine analogy: one button (input) must give one fixed item (output), though two buttons may give the same item. Sort a deck of relation cards into function / not-function and justify each aloud.

misconceptions.description: Confuses codomain with range; says the range of f: R→R, f(x) = x² is R because 'the arrow says R'.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 'R' for any range question when f is declared f: R→R.
misconceptions.remedy: Distinguish 'the set we promise outputs live in' (codomain) from 'outputs actually hit' (range). Compute ranges by asking 'which y truly have a pre-image?' and verify with the graph's shadow on the y-axis.

misconceptions.description: Assumes functions distribute over addition: f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b) for any f.
misconceptions.signal: Writes (x+h)² = x² + h², or √(a+b) = √a + √b when manipulating function values.
misconceptions.remedy: Test the claim numerically on f(x) = x² with a = b = 1 (f(2) = 4 ≠ 2). Classify which functions ARE additive (only f(x) = kx) to convert the error into a theorem.

misconceptions.description: Thinks the domain is always all real numbers, ignoring division-by-zero and negative-radicand restrictions.
misconceptions.signal: States domain R for f(x) = 1/(x−3) or √(x−2) without excluding anything.
misconceptions.remedy: Institute a 'danger scan' checklist before every domain answer: denominators ≠ 0, radicands ≥ 0, log arguments > 0. Evaluate the function at an excluded point on a calculator to see it fail.

real_world_hooks: Aadhaar numbers: each person → exactly one number (a function); person → phone numbers may not be
Auto-rickshaw fare as a function of distance, with its piecewise graph
Postage/parcel pricing as a step (greatest integer) function
Temperature vs time-of-day graphs from the weather app
teaching.video_search: relations and functions domain range class 11

questions.prompt: Let A = {1, 2, 3}. Which of the following relations from A to the set of integers is a FUNCTION on A?

options.diagnosis: Forgot that a function on A must assign an output to EVERY element of A; 3 has no image.

questions.explanation: A function from A must give each element of A exactly one image. {(1,2),(2,3),(3,4)} does. The second and fourth options give some input two different outputs, and the third leaves 3 without any image.

questions.prompt: What is the domain of f(x) = 1/(x² − 4)?

options.diagnosis: Factored x² − 4 only partially; missed the root x = −2 of the difference of squares.
Solved x² − 4 = 0 as x = 4; confused x² = 4 with x = 4.

questions.explanation: The denominator x² − 4 = (x−2)(x+2) is zero at x = 2 and x = −2, so both must be excluded: domain = R − {−2, 2}.

questions.prompt: For f: R → R defined by f(x) = x² + 2, the RANGE of f is:

options.diagnosis: Boundary slip: forgot that x = 0 actually attains the value 2, so 2 belongs to the range.
Gave the range of x² and ignored the vertical shift by +2.

questions.explanation: x² ≥ 0 for all real x, so x² + 2 ≥ 2, and the value 2 is attained at x = 0. The range is [2, ∞) — the codomain R only tells us where outputs are allowed to live, not which are actually reached.

nodes.title: Trigonometric Functions: Radians, Identities, Graphs, Equations
nodes.description: Trigonometry graduates from right-triangle ratios to genuine functions of a real number: angles in radians, the unit circle, signs in all four quadrants, and the wave-like graphs of sine and cosine. You will wield compound-angle and multiple-angle identities like sin(A±B), cos 2x, and solve trigonometric equations in full generality. These functions model every periodic phenomenon — sound, light, tides, alternating current — and their limits and derivatives are pillars of calculus.
learning_outcomes: Can convert between degrees and radians and interpret radian measure as arc length over radius
Can evaluate all six trigonometric functions at standard angles in any quadrant using the unit circle and sign rules
Can sketch and interpret the graphs of sin, cos and tan, identifying period, amplitude and asymptotes
Can apply compound-angle and double-angle identities such as sin(A+B), cos(A+B) and cos 2x to simplify and evaluate expressions
Can write general solutions of equations like sin x = k, cos x = k, tan x = k

misconceptions.description: Distributes trig functions over sums: sin(A + B) = sin A + sin B.
misconceptions.signal: Expands sin(x + 30°) as sin x + sin 30°, or 'cancels' sin across a sum.
misconceptions.remedy: Falsify numerically: sin 90° = 1 but sin 45° + sin 45° = √2. Then motivate the true formula geometrically/with the unit circle, and drill contrast items where both the wrong and right expansions are computed side by side.

misconceptions.description: Ignores the degree/radian distinction; feeds degree values into radian contexts and vice versa.
misconceptions.signal: Says sin 30 = 0.5 with a calculator in radian mode, or uses π = 360° when converting.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor the conversion on π radians = 180° (half turn) and always attach units. Have the student predict sin 30 (radians) vs sin 30° before checking on a calculator, then explain the mismatch.

misconceptions.description: Believes a trigonometric equation has only one solution, forgetting periodicity.
misconceptions.signal: Answers x = π/6 alone for sin x = 1/2, with no nπ or (−1)ⁿ structure.
misconceptions.remedy: Draw the horizontal line y = 1/2 across a long sine graph and count the intersections; then derive the general solution pattern from the graph's symmetry rather than memorising it.

misconceptions.description: Ignores quadrant sign rules, taking all trig ratios positive everywhere.
misconceptions.signal: Writes cos 150° = √3/2, or gives a positive value for sin of a third-quadrant angle.
misconceptions.remedy: Rebuild values from unit-circle coordinates (cos, sin) = (x, y) so signs come from the geometry, not a mnemonic. Then layer the ASTC ('Add Sugar To Chai') summary on top as compression, not as the source of truth.

real_world_hooks: A giant wheel (Ferris wheel) rider's height vs time is a sine curve
AC mains electricity in India: 50 Hz sinusoidal voltage
Sound waves and the pitch of a tanpura string
Day length across the year in Delhi vs Chennai as a cosine wave
ISRO orbital motion: projecting circular motion onto an axis gives sine
teaching.video_search: unit circle trigonometric functions graphs radians class 11

questions.prompt: Convert 150° to radians.

options.diagnosis: Inverted the conversion fraction; multiplied by 180/π instead of π/180.

questions.explanation: Radians = degrees × π/180, so 150° = 150π/180 = 5π/6. Using π = 360° gives the half-sized 5π/12, and simply appending π gives 150π — both come from mishandling the conversion anchor π = 180°.

questions.prompt: If sin x = 3/5, what is the value of cos 2x?

options.diagnosis: Used cos 2x = 2sin²x − 1; the identity's sign structure was flipped.
Found cos x (assuming first quadrant) and stopped; never applied the double-angle step.
Computed cos²x and stopped; used an incomplete double-angle formula.

questions.explanation: cos 2x = 1 − 2sin²x = 1 − 2(9/25) = 1 − 18/25 = 7/25. Note this works regardless of the quadrant of x because only sin²x appears.

questions.prompt: The general solution of sin x = 1/2 is:

options.diagnosis: Applied the cos-equation solution pattern (2nπ ± α) to a sine equation.
Applied the tan-equation pattern (nπ + α); missed the alternating (−1)ⁿ that sine's symmetry requires.

questions.explanation: sin x = 1/2 is satisfied by x = π/6, 5π/6, then repeats every 2π. The compact form x = nπ + (−1)ⁿ π/6 captures both families: n even gives 2kπ + π/6, n odd gives (2k+1)π − π/6 = 2kπ + 5π/6. Checking x = 5π/6 against each option quickly eliminates the wrong patterns.

nodes.title: Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations
nodes.description: To solve x² + 1 = 0 we extend the real numbers with i, where i² = −1, obtaining complex numbers a + bi with their own arithmetic, conjugates and modulus. Quadratic equations with negative discriminant now have two (conjugate) complex roots — the number system finally makes every quadratic solvable. Complex numbers are indispensable in AC circuit analysis, signal processing and quantum physics.
learning_outcomes: Can compute powers of i by reducing exponents modulo 4
Can add, subtract, multiply and divide complex numbers, using the conjugate to rationalise quotients
Can find the modulus and conjugate of a complex number and interpret a + bi as a point in the Argand plane
Can solve quadratic equations with negative discriminant and express roots as conjugate pairs
Can explain why rules like √a·√b = √(ab) fail when both a and b are negative

misconceptions.description: Applies the real-number rule √a·√b = √(ab) to negative radicands: √(−4)·√(−9) = √36 = 6.
misconceptions.signal: Multiplies square roots of negatives without first converting to i-form, getting the sign wrong.
misconceptions.remedy: Enforce the discipline 'convert to i BEFORE any arithmetic': √(−4) = 2i, √(−9) = 3i, product = 6i² = −6. Show that the rule √a√b = √(ab) is only guaranteed when at least one of a, b is non-negative.

misconceptions.description: Believes complex numbers can be ordered: writes 3 + i > 2 + i or asks which of i and 1 is larger.
misconceptions.signal: Uses < or > between non-real complex numbers in working.
misconceptions.remedy: Show geometrically that points in a plane have no single 'left-to-right' order that respects arithmetic; contrast with modulus, which CAN be compared. Prove the classic contradiction: if i > 0 then i² = −1 > 0, absurd; similarly i < 0 fails.

misconceptions.description: Treats i² as +1 (or forgets to simplify i² at all), since 'squaring removes the minus'.
misconceptions.signal: Expands (3+2i)(1−i) and leaves −2i² as −2, or turns it into +... with wrong sign; powers of i computed as if period 2.
misconceptions.remedy: Drill the four-cycle i, −1, −i, 1 on a circle diagram; make the student annotate every i² → −1 substitution explicitly in expansions for a while.

misconceptions.description: Computes modulus as |a + bi| = a + b or a² + b² (forgetting the square root).
misconceptions.signal: Writes |3 + 4i| = 7 or 25 instead of 5.
misconceptions.remedy: Tie modulus to distance in the Argand plane and to Pythagoras: it is the hypotenuse of the (a, b) right triangle. Have the student plot the point and measure before computing.

real_world_hooks: AC circuit impedance in electrical engineering is a complex number
The Argand plane: multiplying by i rotates by 90° — the mathematics of rotation in games and graphics
Signal processing behind JPEG images and MP3 audio uses complex exponentials
The history: Cardano and Bombelli 'imagining' numbers to solve cubics in the 1500s

questions.prompt: The value of i⁴⁵ is:

options.diagnosis: Off-by-one in the four-cycle: used remainder 3 instead of 1 when dividing 45 by 4.
Treated powers of i as alternating with period 2 (odd power → −1).

questions.explanation: Powers of i cycle with period 4: i, −1, −i, 1. Since 45 = 4×11 + 1, i⁴⁵ = (i⁴)¹¹ · i = 1¹¹ · i = i.

questions.prompt: Compute (3 + 2i)(1 − i).

options.diagnosis: Dropped the −2i² term entirely; expanded only three of the four products.
Sign slip combining the middle terms −3i + 2i; concept of i² likely intact.

questions.explanation: (3 + 2i)(1 − i) = 3 − 3i + 2i − 2i² = 3 − i − 2(−1) = 3 − i + 2 = 5 − i. The key move is i² = −1, which turns −2i² into +2.

questions.prompt: The value of √(−4) × √(−9) is:

options.diagnosis: Converted only one of the two radicals to i-form before multiplying.
Converted correctly to 2i·3i but then simplified i² to i; power-of-i slip.

questions.explanation: Convert first: √(−4) = 2i and √(−9) = 3i, so the product is 6i² = −6. The tempting shortcut √(−4)·√(−9) = √36 = 6 is invalid: the rule √a·√b = √(ab) does not hold when both radicands are negative.

nodes.title: Linear Inequalities
nodes.description: Inequalities describe ranges rather than single answers: solving them uses equation-like moves plus one crucial twist — multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. You will express solutions as intervals on the number line and handle systems of simultaneous inequalities. This is the toolkit behind constraints everywhere: budgets, safety limits, eligibility cut-offs, and later, linear programming.
learning_outcomes: Can solve linear inequalities in one variable, reversing the sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative
Can express solution sets in interval notation and graph them on the number line
Can solve a pair of simultaneous inequalities and intersect the solution sets
Can translate word problems (marks, budgets, ranges) into inequalities and interpret the solution in context

misconceptions.description: Forgets to reverse the inequality when multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number.
misconceptions.signal: From −3x > 12 concludes x > −4.
misconceptions.remedy: Test-value habit: after solving, substitute one claimed solution back (x = 0 in −3x > 12 fails instantly). Show on a number line that multiplying by −1 reflects points, which flips left-right order.

misconceptions.description: Treats an inequality like an equation, reporting a single boundary value instead of an interval.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 'x = 2' for 5x − 3 < 3x + 1, or shades nothing on the number line.
misconceptions.remedy: Always demand the answer in three synchronized forms — inequality, interval, number-line shading. Ask 'is 0 a solution? is 1.9? is 2?' to force the set-of-many-values view.

misconceptions.description: For a system of inequalities joined by 'and', takes the union of solution sets instead of the intersection.
misconceptions.signal: Combines x > 1 and x < 4 into 'x > 1 or x < 4' (all reals), or shades both regions fully.
misconceptions.remedy: Overlay the two shaded number lines on transparencies (or two colours) and keep only the doubly-shaded part; connect to intersection of sets from the Sets chapter.

misconceptions.description: Mishandles strict vs non-strict boundaries: includes the endpoint for < or excludes it for ≤.
misconceptions.signal: Writes (−∞, 2] for x < 2, or uses a filled dot for a strict inequality.
misconceptions.remedy: Boundary interrogation: 'does x = 2 itself satisfy 5x − 3 < 3x + 1? Check: 7 < 7 is false.' Make open/closed dot choice a verbalised test, not a guess.

real_world_hooks: Minimum marks needed in the final exam to keep a 75% average
Mobile data plans: for how many GB is Plan A cheaper than Plan B?
IPL auction budgets: spending caps as inequalities
Speed limits and safe-dosage ranges as two-sided inequalities

questions.prompt: Solve for x: −3x > 12.

options.diagnosis: Lost the negative sign on 12/(−3) AND kept the inequality direction; two compounding slips.
Reversed the sign correctly but dropped the negative in −4; arithmetic slip, concept intact.

questions.explanation: Dividing both sides by −3 reverses the inequality: x < 12/(−3) = −4. Sanity check: x = −5 gives −3(−5) = 15 > 12 ✓, while x = 0 gives 0 > 12 ✗.

questions.prompt: The solution set of 5x − 3 < 3x + 1 (x real) is:
questions.explanation: 5x − 3 < 3x + 1 ⟹ 2x < 4 ⟹ x < 2. Dividing by +2 does NOT flip the sign. The boundary 2 is excluded because the inequality is strict: at x = 2 both sides equal 7.

questions.prompt: Ravi scored 65 and 70 in his first two tests. What must he score in the third test (x) so that his average over the three tests is at least 70?

options.diagnosis: Reasoned 'average 70 means each test needs 70'; never set up the average inequality.
Addition slip: took 65 + 70 = 125, giving 210 − 125 = 85; method right, arithmetic wrong.

questions.explanation: (65 + 70 + x)/3 ≥ 70 ⟹ 135 + x ≥ 210 ⟹ x ≥ 75. 'At least 70' includes 70 itself, so the boundary 75 is included: scoring exactly 75 gives an average of exactly 70.

nodes.title: Permutations and Combinations
nodes.description: Counting without listing: the fundamental principle of counting multiplies choices made in sequence, factorials count arrangements, and the twin tools nPr and nCr count ordered selections versus unordered ones. The single most important skill is deciding whether order matters. These techniques power probability, the binomial theorem, and real questions from passwords to tournament fixtures.
learning_outcomes: Can apply the multiplication principle to multi-stage choice problems and the addition principle to exclusive cases
Can compute and manipulate factorials, nPr and nCr, including simplifying quotients of factorials
Can decide from context whether a problem needs permutations (order matters) or combinations (order doesn't)
Can count arrangements with repeated objects (e.g. letters of APPLE) and selections with simple restrictions

misconceptions.description: Uses permutations when order doesn't matter (or combinations when it does) — no test for 'does order count?'.
misconceptions.signal: Computes 10P3 for a committee, or 9C3 for a 3-digit code.
misconceptions.remedy: Institute the two-question checklist before any formula: 'Am I ARRANGING (line, code, ranking → P) or CHOOSING a group (committee, team, handshake → C)?' Verify on a tiny case by explicit listing (choose 2 from {A,B,C}).

misconceptions.description: Adds choices that occur in sequence instead of multiplying them.
misconceptions.signal: For 3 shirts and 4 trousers answers 7 outfits; for a 3-character code adds the options per slot.
misconceptions.remedy: Draw the tree diagram for a small case (2 shirts × 3 trousers) and count the leaves — 6, not 5. Verbalise 'for EACH choice of the first, ALL choices of the second are available → multiply'.

misconceptions.description: Remembers nCr as n!/r!, dropping the (n−r)! factor.
misconceptions.remedy: Rebuild the formula from meaning: arrange r of n things (nPr = n!/(n−r)!), then kill the r! orderings of the chosen group. A quick sanity bound helps: nCr can never exceed 2ⁿ.

misconceptions.description: Counts arrangements of repeated letters as all distinct — no division by the repeats' factorial.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 5! = 120 for arrangements of APPLE.
misconceptions.remedy: Physically label the two P's as P₁, P₂, list arrangements of a 3-letter word with a repeat (e.g. 'MOM'), and watch each real word appear exactly 2! times — motivating division by 2!.

real_world_hooks: Number of possible 4-digit UPI PINs and phone lock patterns
IPL playing XI selection from a 15-member squad (combinations) vs batting order (permutations)
Car number plates: how many in one RTO series?
Round-robin tournament: number of matches = nC2 handshakes
Seating arrangements at a wedding table

questions.prompt: How many 3-digit codes can be formed using the digits 1–9 if no digit repeats?

options.diagnosis: Computed 9³, allowing repeated digits; missed the 'no repetition' condition.

questions.explanation: The three slots have 9, 8, 7 choices respectively (order matters, no repeats): 9 × 8 × 7 = 504 = 9P3. Adding 9 + 8 + 7 = 24 confuses sequential choices with exclusive cases, and 84 = 9C3 ignores that a code is an ORDERED arrangement.

questions.prompt: In how many ways can a committee of 3 members be chosen from 10 people?
questions.explanation: A committee is an unordered group: 10C3 = 10!/(3!·7!) = (10×9×8)/(3×2×1) = 120. 720 = 10P3 counts each committee 3! = 6 times over; 10!/3! forgets the (n−r)! factor; 30 = 10×3 is not a counting principle at all.

questions.prompt: How many distinct arrangements are there of the letters of the word APPLE?

options.diagnosis: Treated the two P's as one letter and computed 4!; collapsed the repeat instead of dividing by 2!.
Divided by 2! twice (or by 4); over-corrected for a single repeated pair.

questions.explanation: APPLE has 5 letters with P repeated twice: 5!/2! = 120/2 = 60. Each genuine word would be counted 2! times if the P's were distinguishable, so we divide 120 by exactly one factor of 2!.

nodes.title: Binomial Theorem
nodes.description: The binomial theorem expands (a + b)ⁿ without multiplying it out: each term is nCr a^(n−r) b^r, with coefficients readable from Pascal's triangle. You will find general terms, middle terms and specific coefficients, and handle expansions like (x − 2y)⁷ where signs alternate. It is the bridge between combinatorics and algebra, and later feeds probability distributions and approximations.
learning_outcomes: Can state and apply the binomial theorem for positive integral n, connecting coefficients to Pascal's triangle and nCr
Can write the general term T(r+1) = nCr a^(n−r) b^r and use it to find any required term or coefficient
Can handle expansions with negative or coefficient-bearing terms like (x − 2y)⁷ and (2x + 3)⁵, applying powers to the whole term
Can count terms in an expansion and locate middle term(s)

misconceptions.description: Believes (a + b)ⁿ = aⁿ + bⁿ — the 'freshman's dream'.
misconceptions.signal: Writes (x + 2)⁵ = x⁵ + 32, or (1.01)ⁿ ≈ 1 + something with no middle terms.
misconceptions.remedy: Falsify with n = 2: (1 + 1)² = 4 ≠ 1² + 1² = 2. Expand (a+b)² and (a+b)³ by hand to SEE the cross terms being born, then present the theorem as bookkeeping for those cross terms.

misconceptions.description: Off-by-one in term indexing: uses r for the r-th term instead of T(r+1) = nCr a^(n−r) b^r, or thinks (a+b)ⁿ has n terms.
misconceptions.signal: For the 4th term uses r = 4; answers 'n terms' when asked how many terms an expansion has.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor on the first term: T₁ corresponds to r = 0, so T(r+1) ↔ r. Have the student write the full expansion of (a+b)³ with r-values 0,1,2,3 labelled under each of its 4 terms.

misconceptions.description: Drops or mishandles the alternating signs in (a − b)ⁿ.
misconceptions.signal: All terms positive in the expansion of (x − 2y)⁷; or negates every term.
misconceptions.remedy: Rewrite (a − b)ⁿ as (a + (−b))ⁿ and carry (−b)^r as a unit; the sign is then (−1)^r, negative exactly for odd r. Check the last term's sign against a quick parity argument.

misconceptions.description: Applies the exponent only to the variable, not the whole term: treats (2x)³ as 2x³.
misconceptions.signal: Coefficient answers off by powers of 2 or 3 in expansions like (2x + 3)⁵.
misconceptions.remedy: Force bracket discipline: write every general term as nCr (2x)^(n−r) (3)^r with brackets intact, and evaluate the numeric parts in a separate line before combining.

real_world_hooks: Pascal's triangle appears in Pingala's ancient Indian prosody (Meru Prastara) — counting syllable patterns
Compound interest growth (1 + r)ⁿ and quick approximations like (1.01)¹⁰
Probability of k heads in n coin tosses uses binomial coefficients
Genetics: offspring trait combinations follow binomial patterns

questions.prompt: How many terms are there in the expansion of (x + y)⁴?

options.diagnosis: Computed 2⁴ — confused the VALUE of (1+1)⁴ (sum of coefficients) with the number of terms.
Off-by-one in the other direction (n + 2); knows there's a '+1' somewhere but misplaced it.

questions.explanation: (x + y)ⁿ expands into terms for r = 0, 1, ..., n — that's n + 1 terms. For n = 4: x⁴, 4x³y, 6x²y², 4xy³, y⁴ — five terms.

questions.prompt: The coefficient of x² in the expansion of (x + 2)⁵ is:

options.diagnosis: Multiplied 5C2 by 2 instead of 2³; applied the wrong power to the constant.

questions.explanation: General term: 5Cr x^(5−r) 2^r. For x² we need 5 − r = 2, so r = 3: T₄ = 5C3 · x² · 2³ = 10 × 8 × x² = 80x². Forgetting the 2³ gives 10; using r = 2 (off-by-one) gives 5C2·2² = 40.

questions.prompt: The 4th term in the expansion of (x − 2y)⁷ is:
questions.explanation: T₄ = T(3+1) = 7C3 x⁴ (−2y)³ = 35 · x⁴ · (−8y³) = −280x⁴y³. The whole bracket (−2y) is cubed — giving −8, not −2 — and r = 3 (not 4) for the fourth term.

nodes.title: Sequences and Series: AP, GP, AM-GM, Special Sums
nodes.description: Sequences follow rules; series add them up. Building on arithmetic progressions, you now master geometric progressions — nth term arⁿ⁻¹, finite sums, and the beautiful infinite sum a/(1−r) when |r| < 1 — plus the AM ≥ GM inequality and formulas for Σn, Σn², Σn³. Growth by a constant ratio is the mathematics of compound interest, population growth and radioactive decay.
learning_outcomes: Can identify whether a sequence is an AP, a GP or neither, and find common difference/ratio
Can compute the nth term and the sum of n terms of a GP, and insert geometric means
Can determine when an infinite GP has a finite sum and compute S∞ = a/(1−r)
Can apply AM ≥ GM for two positive numbers and use Σn, Σn², Σn³ to evaluate special series

misconceptions.description: Applies AP formulas to a GP (or vice versa): uses a + (n−1)d on a sequence that multiplies.
misconceptions.signal: For 3, 6, 12, ... writes the 10th term as 3 + 9×3; treats the ratio as a difference.
misconceptions.remedy: Train the first move: compute both consecutive differences AND consecutive ratios for the first three terms; only one will be constant. Say the recipe aloud: 'constant difference → add; constant ratio → multiply'.

misconceptions.description: Off-by-one in term formulas: uses arⁿ or a + nd instead of arⁿ⁻¹ or a + (n−1)d.
misconceptions.signal: Answers are exactly one factor of r (or one d) too large; the 1st term formula gives the 2nd term.
misconceptions.remedy: Test every formula at n = 1: it must return a itself. Build the pattern from a table (term 1: a·r⁰, term 2: a·r¹, ...) so the exponent 'n−1' is seen as 'number of jumps from the start'.

misconceptions.description: Believes every infinite GP has a finite sum, applying a/(1−r) even when |r| ≥ 1.
misconceptions.signal: Computes S∞ for 2 + 4 + 8 + ... as 2/(1−2) = −2 and accepts a negative 'sum' of positive terms.
misconceptions.remedy: Have the student add partial sums of 2 + 4 + 8 + ... and watch them explode, then of 8 + 4 + 2 + ... and watch them settle. Make '|r| < 1?' a mandatory pre-flight check before S∞, and celebrate the absurd −2 as a warning story.

misconceptions.description: Uses AM ≥ GM without checking positivity, or believes AM = GM for any pair.
misconceptions.signal: Applies AM-GM to negative numbers; claims (a+b)/2 = √(ab) generally.
misconceptions.remedy: Compute both means for pairs like (1, 9) → AM 5, GM 3 to see strict inequality; identify equality holds only when the numbers are equal; show √(ab) is not even real for a = −1, b = 4.

real_world_hooks: The rice-on-a-chessboard legend: doubling grains is a GP that bankrupts a king
Compound interest and SIP mutual-fund growth are GPs
A ball bouncing to 3/4 of its height each time: total distance is an infinite GP
Viral videos and chain messages: each share triggers r more shares
Radioactive decay and drug concentration in the bloodstream

questions.prompt: The 10th term of the GP 3, 6, 12, 24, ... is:

options.diagnosis: Computed 2⁹ but forgot to multiply by the first term a = 3.

questions.explanation: a = 3, r = 2, so T₁₀ = ar⁹ = 3 × 2⁹ = 3 × 512 = 1536. Using r¹⁰ gives 3072 (off-by-one), and treating the sequence as an AP with 'd = 3' gives 3 + 9×3 = 30.

questions.prompt: The sum of the first 20 terms of the AP with first term 2 and common difference 3 is:

options.diagnosis: Used n instead of n/2 in Sₙ = (n/2)[2a + (n−1)d]; forgot to halve.
Halved twice — applied n/2 and then divided the final answer by 2 again.

questions.explanation: S₂₀ = (20/2)[2(2) + 19(3)] = 10 × (4 + 57) = 10 × 61 = 610. Using 20 jumps (20×3) instead of 19 gives 640; the n/2 factor comes from pairing terms, and must appear exactly once.

questions.prompt: The sum to infinity of the series 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + ... is:

options.diagnosis: Believes any infinite series must diverge; hasn't internalised convergence for |r| < 1.
Added only the displayed terms (8 + 4 + 2) — computed a partial sum, not the limit.
Multiplied by (1 − r) instead of dividing: computed a(1 − r) = 8 × 1/2.

questions.explanation: Here a = 8 and r = 1/2 with |r| < 1, so S∞ = a/(1 − r) = 8/(1 − 1/2) = 16. Geometrically: 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 0.5 + ... creeps up to, but never passes, 16 — the halves exactly fill the gap.

nodes.title: Straight Lines: Slope, Forms of Equations, Distance
nodes.description: Coordinate geometry turns lines into equations: slope measures steepness as tan of the inclination, and a line can be written in point-slope, two-point, slope-intercept, intercept or general form. Parallel lines share slopes; perpendicular slopes multiply to −1; and the distance from a point to a line has a crisp formula. This algebra-geometry dictionary is the foundation for conic sections, calculus tangents, and linear programming.
learning_outcomes: Can compute the slope of a line from two points or from its inclination, and interpret zero vs undefined slope
Can write the equation of a line in point-slope, slope-intercept, two-point, intercept and general forms and convert between them
Can apply parallelism (equal slopes) and perpendicularity (m₁m₂ = −1) conditions
Can compute the distance from a point to a line and the distance between parallel lines

misconceptions.description: Confuses zero slope with undefined slope: thinks a vertical line has slope 0.
misconceptions.signal: Writes m = 0 for x = 3, or tries y = mx + c form for a vertical line.
misconceptions.remedy: Walk the line physically: flat road = zero slope (no rise), sheer wall = can't walk it, rise/run divides by zero. Pair the graphs of y = 2 and x = 3 and compute rise/run for each from two actual points.

misconceptions.description: Thinks perpendicular lines have equal (or merely reciprocal) slopes instead of m₁m₂ = −1.
misconceptions.signal: Gives the same slope, or the reciprocal without the sign flip, for a perpendicular line.
misconceptions.remedy: Rotate a set square on a coordinate grid: as one arm's slope is 2/3, measure the other's as −3/2. Verify m₁ × m₂ = −1 numerically for several drawn pairs before using it abstractly.

misconceptions.description: Inverts slope as run/rise: Δx/Δy instead of Δy/Δx.
misconceptions.signal: Slope answers are reciprocals of the correct value; steep lines get small slopes.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor slope to meaning: 'how much y changes per unit of x' — like speed is distance per time, not time per distance. Check against steepness intuition: a near-vertical line must have LARGE |m|.

misconceptions.description: Reads slope off an unsolved general form: for 2x + 3y = 6 takes m = 2 (the x-coefficient).
misconceptions.signal: States the slope of ax + by + c = 0 as a, skipping the rearrangement to y = mx + c.
misconceptions.remedy: Make 'solve for y first' a reflex, then derive the shortcut m = −a/b once and verify it against two rearranged examples so the sign and ratio are understood, not guessed.

real_world_hooks: Ramp gradients for wheelchair access (building codes specify maximum slope)
Taxi/auto fare vs distance: slope = rate per km, intercept = base fare
Railway gradients through the Ghats expressed as 1 in 40
Straight-line depreciation of a laptop's value over years
Cricket run-rate charts: required rate as the slope of a chase line

questions.prompt: The slope of the line through the points (1, 2) and (3, 8) is:

options.diagnosis: Computed the rise (8 − 2) but never divided by the run; incomplete formula.
Mixed the subtraction order — used (8 − 2)/(1 − 3); consistency of order slipped.

questions.explanation: m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = (8 − 2)/(3 − 1) = 6/2 = 3. The coordinate order must match in numerator and denominator, and the ratio is rise over run — not run over rise.

questions.prompt: The slope of a line PERPENDICULAR to the line 2x + 3y = 6 is:

options.diagnosis: Took the reciprocal but mishandled the sign flip; m₁m₂ = (−2/3)(−3/2) = +1 ≠ −1.

questions.explanation: Rearranged: y = (−2/3)x + 2, so the given slope is −2/3. Perpendicular slope = negative reciprocal = 3/2 (check: (−2/3)(3/2) = −1 ✓). Reading m = 2 straight off 2x + 3y = 6 leads to the wrong −1/2.

questions.prompt: The distance of the point (3, −5) from the line 3x − 4y − 26 = 0 is:

options.diagnosis: Forgot to divide by √(a² + b²) = 5; used only the numerator |3x₁ − 4y₁ − 26|.
Sign slip substituting y = −5: computed 9 − 20 − 26 instead of 9 + 20 − 26.
Dropped the minus on 26 (used +26) and skipped the denominator; formula recalled only in fragments.

questions.explanation: d = |3(3) − 4(−5) − 26| / √(3² + (−4)²) = |9 + 20 − 26| / 5 = 3/5. Watch the double negative: −4 × (−5) = +20, and always divide by √(a² + b²).

nodes.title: Conic Sections: Circle, Parabola, Ellipse, Hyperbola
nodes.description: Slice a double cone at different angles and you get circles, parabolas, ellipses and hyperbolas — a single family of curves with standard equations: x² + y² = r², y² = 4ax, x²/a² + y²/b² = 1, x²/a² − y²/b² = 1. You will extract centres, foci, vertices, directrices, axes and eccentricity from these equations. Conics are the shapes of planetary orbits, satellite dishes, headlight reflectors and suspension-bridge cables.
learning_outcomes: Can write the equation of a circle from centre and radius, and complete the square to find them from the general form
Can identify the focus, directrix, axis and latus rectum of a parabola in any of the four standard orientations
Can find vertices, foci, eccentricity and axes lengths for ellipses and hyperbolas in standard form, using c² = a² − b² or c² = a² + b² appropriately
Can classify which conic a given second-degree equation in standard form represents

misconceptions.description: Mixes the focal relations: uses c² = a² + b² for an ellipse (or c² = a² − b² for a hyperbola).
misconceptions.signal: Gets foci outside the ellipse, e.g. (±√34, 0) for x²/25 + y²/9 = 1.
misconceptions.remedy: Tie the relation to geometry: an ellipse's foci are INSIDE (c < a, so subtract); a hyperbola's are beyond the vertices (c > a, so add). Sanity-check every answer by plotting: elliptical foci must lie within the curve.

misconceptions.description: In y² = 4ax, reads the coefficient 4a as a itself, misplacing focus and directrix by a factor of 4.
misconceptions.signal: For y² = 12x states the focus as (12, 0) instead of (3, 0).
misconceptions.remedy: Always solve 4a = coefficient explicitly as a labelled step. Verify with the latus rectum: the chord through the claimed focus should have length 4a = 12 — plugging x = 3 gives y = ±6 ✓, x = 12 fails.

misconceptions.description: Assumes any equation containing both x² and y² is a circle.
misconceptions.signal: Calls x² + 2y² = 4 or x² − y² = 4 a circle.
misconceptions.remedy: Sort a stack of equations by the checklist: equal coefficients & plus sign → circle; unequal & plus → ellipse; minus → hyperbola; only one square → parabola. Graph one of each so the algebraic tags map to distinct shapes.

misconceptions.description: Detaches eccentricity from shape: accepts e > 1 for an ellipse or e = 1 for one, mixing the ranges up.
misconceptions.signal: Reports an ellipse with e = 1.3 without flinching; can't say which conic e = 1 signals.
misconceptions.remedy: Build the e-dial: e = 0 circle → 0 < e < 1 ellipse → e = 1 parabola → e > 1 hyperbola, with a morphing animation. Interpret e as 'how far from circular', so e > 1 for an ellipse becomes visibly impossible.

real_world_hooks: ISRO transfer orbits: satellites move on ellipses with Earth at a focus
Dish TV antennas and solar cookers are parabolic — parallel rays meet at the focus
A cricket ball's flight is (nearly) a parabola
Torch beam on a wall: tilt it and watch circle → ellipse → parabola → hyperbola
LORAN ship navigation uses hyperbolas of constant time-difference

questions.prompt: The focus of the parabola y² = 12x is at:

options.diagnosis: Right value of a but wrong axis — y² = 4ax opens along the x-axis, not the y-axis.
Direction slip: positive coefficient means the parabola opens right, focus on the positive x-axis.

questions.explanation: Compare y² = 12x with y² = 4ax: 4a = 12, so a = 3. The parabola opens rightward with focus (a, 0) = (3, 0) and directrix x = −3.

questions.prompt: The foci of the ellipse x²/25 + y²/9 = 1 are:

options.diagnosis: Used a itself as the focal distance — those are the vertices, not the foci.
Correct c but wrong axis; the major axis lies along x since 25 > 9.

questions.explanation: a² = 25, b² = 9, and for an ellipse c² = a² − b² = 16, so c = 4. The major axis is along x (larger denominator under x²), giving foci (±4, 0). Adding instead of subtracting (c = √34 > a) would absurdly place the foci outside the ellipse.

questions.prompt: The equation x² + 2y² = 4 represents:

options.diagnosis: Associated 'two squared terms with different coefficients' with hyperbola; the minus sign, not unequal coefficients, is the hyperbola's signature.
Treats any second-degree curve as a parabola; a parabola has exactly ONE squared variable.

questions.explanation: Divide by 4: x²/4 + y²/2 = 1 — a sum of two squared terms with UNEQUAL positive denominators, i.e. an ellipse (a² = 4, b² = 2). A circle needs equal coefficients; a hyperbola needs a minus sign; a parabola has only one squared variable.

nodes.title: Introduction to Three-Dimensional Geometry
nodes.description: Adding a z-axis turns the coordinate plane into coordinate space: points become ordered triples (x, y, z), space splits into eight octants, and the familiar tools upgrade — distance becomes √(Δx² + Δy² + Δz²) and the section formula gains a third coordinate. Thinking in 3D coordinates is the gateway to vectors, planes and lines in space, and to how GPS, drones and graphics engines locate anything in the world.
learning_outcomes: Can locate and interpret points (x, y, z), including which coordinate planes and octants they relate to
Can state the coordinates of points on the axes and coordinate planes (which coordinates vanish where)
Can compute the distance between two points in space and use it to classify triangles or verify collinearity
Can apply the section formula (internal division) and midpoint formula in 3D

misconceptions.description: Uses the 2D distance formula in 3D, silently dropping the z-term.
misconceptions.signal: Computes √(Δx² + Δy²) for points with different z-coordinates.
misconceptions.remedy: Derive the 3D formula as Pythagoras applied twice — the box diagonal: floor diagonal first, then up the wall. Have the student compute the diagonal of an actual room to make the third term unforgettable.

misconceptions.description: Mixes up which coordinate vanishes where: thinks a point on the xy-plane has x = 0 or y = 0 (rather than z = 0), or confuses distance-from-plane with distance-from-axis.
misconceptions.signal: Says (2, 3, 0) lies on the z-axis, or that the z-coordinate is the distance from the z-axis.
misconceptions.remedy: Use the classroom corner as the origin: two walls and the floor are the coordinate planes. Physically point: on the floor (xy-plane) you can move in x and y but z = 0. The 'missing' coordinate is the one measuring how far you've LEFT that plane.

misconceptions.description: Misapplies the section formula: swaps which endpoint gets which ratio part, or averages when a ratio is given.
misconceptions.signal: For a 2:1 division gets the point closer to the wrong end; uses the midpoint formula regardless of ratio.
misconceptions.remedy: Mark the segment on a number line first and estimate where 2:1 should fall (two-thirds of the way). The estimate then arbitrates between (2x₂ + x₁)/3 and (2x₁ + x₂)/3 — the ratio parts attach to the OPPOSITE endpoints.

real_world_hooks: The corner of your room as the origin: walls and floor are the coordinate planes
Drone delivery: latitude, longitude, altitude is an (x, y, z) triple
Air traffic control tracks planes in 3D coordinates
3D printers move a nozzle to (x, y, z) positions layer by layer
Chandrayaan's position relative to the lunar surface needs three numbers
teaching.video_search: three dimensional geometry octants distance formula class 11

questions.prompt: A point lies on the xy-plane. Which of its coordinates must be zero?

options.text: None — a point on a plane can have any coordinates
options.diagnosis: Hasn't connected 'lying on a coordinate plane' with a coordinate constraint at all; rebuild with the room-corner model.

questions.explanation: The xy-plane is the 'floor' containing the x- and y-axes; height above it is measured by z. Points on it have z = 0 — the vanishing coordinate is the one NOT named in the plane.

questions.prompt: The distance between the points (1, 2, 3) and (3, 5, 9) is:

options.diagnosis: Computed the sum of squared differences but forgot the final square root.
Squared the z-difference as 6×2 = 12 instead of 6² = 36; got √25 = 5.

questions.explanation: d = √((3−1)² + (5−2)² + (9−3)²) = √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7. Dropping the z-term gives √13 — the 2D shadow of the true distance.

questions.prompt: The point dividing the segment from A(2, −1, 3) to B(5, 2, 9) internally in the ratio 2 : 1 is:

options.diagnosis: Ignored the given ratio and computed the midpoint (1:1 division).
Used the EXTERNAL division formula (m·B − n·A)/(m − n) for an internal division.

questions.explanation: Internal division m:n = 2:1 from A to B: P = ((2·5 + 1·2)/3, (2·2 + 1·(−1))/3, (2·9 + 1·3)/3) = (4, 1, 7). Note P is two-thirds of the way to B, matching the 2:1 estimate; (3, 0, 5) is the 1:2 point — ratio attached to the wrong ends.

nodes.title: Limits and Derivatives
nodes.description: Calculus begins here: a limit captures the value a function approaches — which may exist even where the function itself is undefined, as in (x²−4)/(x−2) at x = 2. The derivative is a limit of slopes of secants, giving the exact instantaneous rate of change and the slope of the tangent line. You will evaluate algebraic and trigonometric limits (including sin x/x → 1), differentiate from first principles, and use the sum, product and quotient rules. Every 'rate' in science — velocity, current, growth — is a derivative.
learning_outcomes: Can explain a limit intuitively via left- and right-hand approach, and evaluate limits by substitution where valid
Can resolve 0/0 forms by factoring, rationalising, or standard limits like lim (xⁿ−aⁿ)/(x−a) = naⁿ⁻¹ and lim sin x/x = 1
Can compute a derivative from first principles as the limit of a difference quotient
Can interpret the derivative as instantaneous rate of change and as the slope of the tangent line
Can differentiate polynomials and trigonometric functions using sum, product and quotient rules

misconceptions.description: Equates limit with function value: believes lim x→a f(x) is just f(a), and cannot exist if f(a) is undefined.
misconceptions.signal: Declares lim x→2 (x²−4)/(x−2) 'undefined because you can't put x = 2'.
misconceptions.remedy: Tabulate f at 1.9, 1.99, 1.999 and 2.1, 2.01, 2.001 and watch the values crowd around 4 while f(2) itself doesn't exist. Language shift: the limit is about the JOURNEY (approach), not the destination point.

misconceptions.description: Treats the 0/0 form as an answer: 'it equals 0', 'it equals 1', or 'the limit does not exist'.
misconceptions.signal: Stops at substitution, reports DNE or 0 whenever numerator and denominator both vanish.
misconceptions.remedy: Rebrand 0/0 as 'indeterminate = investigate further', never a verdict. Show three limits that are all 0/0 on substitution yet equal 4, 0 and ∞ respectively, proving the form alone decides nothing.

misconceptions.description: Differentiates products term-by-term: (fg)' = f'g'.
misconceptions.signal: Writes d/dx (x² sin x) = 2x cos x.
misconceptions.remedy: Counterexample first: (x · x)' = (x²)' = 2x, but f'g' = 1·1 = 1. Then motivate the product rule via the growing-rectangle picture (area change = f·Δg + g·Δf) and drill with the 'each factor takes a turn being differentiated' chant.

misconceptions.description: Confuses average rate (secant slope) with instantaneous rate (tangent slope), or computes slope as y/x from the origin.
misconceptions.signal: Answers rate questions with f(b)−f(a) over b−a when the instantaneous rate at a point is asked; divides f(a) by a.
misconceptions.remedy: Zoom-in animation: secants through shrinking intervals visibly rotate into the tangent. Speedometer vs trip-average analogy: 'what does the speedometer read AT this instant?' is the derivative question.

real_world_hooks: Speedometer vs average speed on a Mumbai–Pune drive: instantaneous vs average rate
A batsman's strike rate over the whole innings vs 'momentum' this over
ISRO rocket velocity as the derivative of altitude during launch
Zeno's paradox: how can approaching forever add up to arriving?
COVID case curves: 'the rate of new cases is slowing' is a statement about a derivative
teaching.video_search: limits and derivatives first principles tangent slope class 11

questions.prompt: Evaluate lim x→2 (x² − 4)/(x − 2).

options.diagnosis: Cancelled to x instead of x + 2 — factoring slip (x² − 4 = (x−2)(x+2)).

questions.explanation: Substitution gives 0/0 — indeterminate, so investigate: (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = (x−2)(x+2)/(x−2) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2, and lim x→2 (x + 2) = 4. The function is undefined AT 2, yet its limit there exists and equals 4.

questions.prompt: The derivative of x² sin x is:

options.diagnosis: Differentiated only sin x and left x² as a passive constant; product rule not triggered.
Product rule structure right but inserted a minus — possibly contaminated by the quotient rule's numerator.

questions.explanation: Product rule: (fg)' = f'g + fg' with f = x², g = sin x: 2x sin x + x² cos x. Multiplying the separate derivatives (2x)(cos x) is the classic trap — check it fails even for x·x.

questions.prompt: Evaluate lim x→0 sin 4x / x.

options.diagnosis: Pattern-matched 'sin(something)/x = 1' without matching the arguments; the standard limit needs sin 4x over 4x.
Rescaled in the wrong direction — divided by 4 instead of multiplying.

questions.explanation: Write sin 4x/x = 4 · sin 4x/(4x). As x→0, 4x→0, so sin 4x/(4x) → 1, and the limit is 4 × 1 = 4. The standard limit sin θ/θ → 1 applies only when the SAME expression sits inside sin and underneath.

nodes.title: Statistics: Measures of Dispersion, Variance, Standard Deviation
nodes.description: Two datasets can share a mean yet behave completely differently — dispersion measures how spread out the data is. You will compute range, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation for ungrouped and grouped data, and compare the consistency of two datasets using the coefficient of variation. Standard deviation is the workhorse of real analytics, from batting consistency to quality control and finance risk.
learning_outcomes: Can compute range, mean deviation (about mean or median), variance and standard deviation for ungrouped and grouped data
Can explain why deviations are squared (or absolute-valued) — raw deviations from the mean always sum to zero
Can predict the effect on mean, variance and SD of adding a constant to, or scaling, every observation
Can compare consistency of two datasets with different means using the coefficient of variation CV = (σ/x̄)×100

misconceptions.description: Conflates variance and standard deviation — reports σ² when σ is asked, or thinks SD can be negative.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 8 when the SD is 2√2; is untroubled by a 'negative SD' after a sign error.
misconceptions.remedy: Emphasise units: if data is in cm, variance is in cm² but SD is back in cm — that's the whole point of the square root. Make writing units after both quantities mandatory for a while; a negative or squared-unit SD then self-flags.

misconceptions.description: Averages raw (signed) deviations from the mean and is puzzled by (or ignores) the inevitable zero.
misconceptions.signal: Computes mean deviation without absolute values, gets 0, and either reports it or fudges signs arbitrarily.
misconceptions.remedy: Prove Σ(xᵢ − x̄) = 0 with a see-saw/balance-point picture: the mean is precisely where deviations cancel. Then present |·| and squaring as the two standard fixes, leading to mean deviation and variance respectively.

misconceptions.description: Compares consistency across datasets using raw SD even when the means differ wildly, instead of the coefficient of variation.
misconceptions.signal: Says the dataset with the smaller SD is 'more consistent' regardless of scale (₹100-scale vs ₹10,000-scale data).
misconceptions.remedy: Show a salary dataset (mean 50,000, SD 500) vs a pocket-money dataset (mean 100, SD 50): smaller SD yet wilder relative swings. Institute the rule: different means → divide out the scale → compare CV = σ/x̄.

misconceptions.description: Thinks shifting every observation by a constant changes the spread: SD(x + 5) = SD(x) + 5.
misconceptions.signal: Adds the constant to the SD after a data-shift question; recomputes everything from scratch and still errs.
misconceptions.remedy: Slide a dot-plot bodily 5 units right on screen: gaps between points are visibly unchanged, so every deviation xᵢ − x̄ survives intact. Contrast with SCALING by k, which stretches gaps and multiplies SD by |k|.

real_world_hooks: Kohli vs a hit-or-miss opener: same average, different SD — who do you pick for a final?
Monsoon rainfall variability across Indian cities with similar annual totals
Quality control: a biscuit factory tracking weight SD on the production line
Mutual fund risk: SD of returns is literally the 'volatility' in the fact sheet
Class marks: same average in two sections, very different spreads

questions.prompt: The variance of the data 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 is:

options.diagnosis: Summed the squared deviations but forgot to divide by n = 5.

questions.explanation: Mean = 6. Deviations: −4, −2, 0, 2, 4; squares: 16, 4, 0, 4, 16, summing to 40. Variance = 40/5 = 8 (and SD = √8 = 2√2). Raw deviations sum to 0 — which is why we square them first.

questions.prompt: Each observation in a dataset is increased by 5. The standard deviation of the new dataset:

options.diagnosis: Half-remembered transformation rule — knows 'something non-obvious happens' but SD is exactly unchanged under shifts.
Confused adding a constant with multiplying by one; scaling by k is what multiplies SD by |k|.

questions.explanation: Adding a constant shifts every value AND the mean by 5, so each deviation xᵢ − x̄ is untouched — SD unchanged. (The mean increases by 5; only multiplying the data by k rescales the SD.)

questions.prompt: Batsman A has mean score 50 with SD 5; batsman B has mean score 25 with SD 4. Who is more consistent?

options.text: A, because A's coefficient of variation (10%) is lower than B's (16%)
B, because B's SD (4) is smaller than A's (5)
B, because smaller scores fluctuate less in general
options.diagnosis: Judging consistency by the size of the mean itself; neither SD nor mean alone measures relative spread.

options.text: Both are equally consistent since 4 and 5 are nearly equal
options.diagnosis: Treats close raw SDs as equivalent — hasn't normalised by the very different means.

questions.explanation: Consistency across different scoring levels is compared by CV = (σ/x̄)×100: A → (5/50)×100 = 10%, B → (4/25)×100 = 16%. A's scores wobble only 10% of his average, so A is more consistent despite the larger raw SD.

nodes.title: Probability: Random Experiments and the Axiomatic Approach
nodes.description: Probability is rebuilt on set theory: a random experiment has a sample space, events are subsets, and probability is a function obeying three axioms — non-negativity, P(S) = 1, and additivity for mutually exclusive events. From these flow the complement rule P(not A) = 1 − P(A) and the addition rule P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B). This foundation supports everything from weather forecasts to insurance and machine learning.
learning_outcomes: Can describe sample spaces and events as sets for experiments like coin tosses, dice and card draws
Can identify mutually exclusive and exhaustive events and state the axioms of probability
Can apply the complement rule and the addition rule P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B)
Can combine counting techniques (permutations/combinations) with equally-likely outcomes to compute probabilities
Can recognise impossible probability values (outside [0, 1])

misconceptions.description: Equiprobability bias: treats every event as 50-50 ('it either happens or it doesn't') or all outcomes as equally likely even when they aren't.
misconceptions.signal: Says P(rolling a number > 4) = 1/2 'because it happens or it doesn't'; assigns 1/3 each to win/lose/draw in any match.
misconceptions.remedy: Expose the bias with the two-dice sum experiment: sums 2–12 are NOT equally likely (tally 100 rolls, 7 dominates). Enforce the discipline of listing the actual sample space and checking the symmetry claim before dividing counts.

misconceptions.description: Adds probabilities of non-mutually-exclusive events without subtracting the overlap: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) always.
misconceptions.signal: Gets P > 1 for 'king or heart' type questions and doesn't flinch; never mentions P(A∩B).
misconceptions.remedy: Venn-diagram the card deck: shade kings and hearts, watch the king-of-hearts get shaded twice. Tie directly to n(A∪B) from Sets; make 'are they mutually exclusive?' the first written line of every addition-rule solution.

misconceptions.description: Accepts probability values outside [0, 1], e.g. P = 1.4 or P = −0.2, after mechanical arithmetic.
misconceptions.signal: Reports a probability greater than 1 or negative without noticing the impossibility.
misconceptions.remedy: Build the reflex: every probability answer gets range-checked against the axioms before writing it down. Interpret endpoints concretely — 0 = impossible, 1 = certain — so 1.4 reads as 'more certain than certain', an obvious absurdity.

misconceptions.description: Confuses mutually exclusive with exhaustive (or with independent): thinks disjoint events must cover everything, or that 'can't happen together' means 'unrelated'.
misconceptions.signal: Claims P(A) + P(B) = 1 whenever A, B are mutually exclusive; uses the words interchangeably.
misconceptions.remedy: Sort event pairs on a die into a 2×2 grid (exclusive? exhaustive?) with an example in every cell — e.g. {1} and {2} are exclusive but far from exhaustive. Vocabulary precision drills with justification aloud.

real_world_hooks: DLS method and win predictors in cricket broadcasts are probability statements
Ludo and Snakes-and-Ladders: dice sample spaces you've known for years
IMD's '70% chance of rain' — what does it actually claim?
Insurance premiums priced off probabilities of events
Lottery and lucky-draw odds: why the intuition 'I either win or lose' misleads

questions.prompt: A fair die is thrown once. The probability of getting a number greater than 4 is:

options.diagnosis: Counted 'greater than or equal to 4' — boundary slip including 4 itself... and then miscounted; {4,5,6} would give 1/2, {5,6} gives 1/3. Re-examine which outcomes qualify.
Counted only one favourable outcome; treated 'greater than 4' as 'equal to 5' or 'equal to 6' alone.

questions.explanation: Favourable outcomes: {5, 6} — two of the six equally likely faces, so P = 2/6 = 1/3. 'It happens or it doesn't' does NOT make it 1/2; the outcomes, not the descriptions, must be equally likely.

questions.prompt: Given P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A∩B) = 0.2, find P(A∪B).

options.diagnosis: Reported the intersection instead of the union; 'or' and 'and' swapped.
Subtracted everything in sight (0.5 − 0.4 + ... ); formula structure not yet stable.

questions.explanation: P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B) = 0.4 + 0.5 − 0.2 = 0.7. Adding without subtracting the overlap double-counts outcomes in both A and B.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is tossed three times. What is the probability of getting at least one head?

options.diagnosis: Computed P(exactly one head); 'at least one' includes one, two or three heads.
Found the complement P(no heads) correctly but forgot the final step 1 − 1/8.

questions.explanation: The complement of 'at least one head' is 'no heads' = TTT, with probability (1/2)³ = 1/8. So P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8. The complement shortcut beats listing all 8 outcomes — but you must finish the subtraction.

nodes.title: Relations and Functions: Types, Composition, Invertibility
nodes.description: Functions acquire structure: relations can be reflexive, symmetric, transitive (equivalence relations), and functions can be one-one (injective), onto (surjective) or both (bijective). Composition chains functions together — (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)) — and exactly the bijective functions can be undone by an inverse. Invertibility is the deep idea behind every 'decode', 'undo' and 'solve for x' in mathematics, and behind encryption itself.
learning_outcomes: Can test a relation for reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity and identify equivalence relations and their classes
Can prove or disprove that a function is one-one and/or onto, with counterexamples where needed
Can compute compositions g∘f and f∘g, respecting order, and give examples where they differ
Can decide whether a function is invertible and find f⁻¹ explicitly for simple bijections
Can restrict domain/codomain to make a non-invertible function invertible

misconceptions.description: Misreads composition: thinks (g∘f)(x) means g(x)·f(x), or that composition is commutative (f∘g = g∘f).
misconceptions.signal: Multiplies the two function values; computes f(g(x)) when g(f(x)) is asked and expects the same answer.
misconceptions.remedy: Machine-chain picture: f's output conveyor feeds g's input hopper — order is physical. Compute both f∘g and g∘f for f(x) = x+2, g(x) = 3x and display the different results side by side; read g∘f aloud as 'g AFTER f'.

misconceptions.description: Confuses the inverse function with the reciprocal: f⁻¹(x) = 1/f(x).
misconceptions.signal: Writes f⁻¹(x) = 1/(3x − 4) for f(x) = 3x − 4; reads sin⁻¹ as cosec.
misconceptions.remedy: Contrast the two meanings of the exponent −1 on numbers vs functions explicitly. Define f⁻¹ operationally — 'the machine run backwards' — and always verify by composing: f⁻¹(f(x)) must return x, which 1/f(x) spectacularly fails.

misconceptions.description: Believes every function has an inverse, skipping the bijectivity requirement.
misconceptions.signal: Confidently 'inverts' f(x) = x² on R to get √x; never checks one-one or onto.
misconceptions.remedy: Run the backwards machine on f(x) = x²: input 4 — should the output be 2 or −2? The ambiguity IS the failure of one-one. Then show the standard repair (restrict to x ≥ 0), making bijectivity feel like a needed licence, not red tape.

misconceptions.description: Garbles 'one-one' as 'each input has one output' (the definition of a function) rather than distinct inputs having distinct outputs.
misconceptions.signal: Declares f(x) = x² one-one 'because every x gives exactly one x²'.
misconceptions.remedy: Sharpen with arrow diagrams: function-ness is about arrows LEAVING each input (exactly one); one-one is about arrows ARRIVING at each output (at most one). The horizontal line test makes the second condition visual.

real_world_hooks: Encryption/decryption: WhatsApp messages need functions that CAN be undone by exactly one key
Aadhaar enrolment: person → number must be one-one for de-duplication to work
Currency conversion INR→USD and back: composing a function with its inverse
'Same birthday' as a relation on your class: reflexive? symmetric? transitive?
QR codes: encode then decode is f followed by f⁻¹

questions.prompt: Let f(x) = x + 2 and g(x) = 3x. Find (g∘f)(2).

options.diagnosis: Added f(2) + g(2) = 4 + 6; invented an operation instead of composing.

questions.explanation: (g∘f)(2) = g(f(2)) = g(4) = 12 — apply f FIRST, then feed its output to g. Reversing the order gives (f∘g)(2) = f(6) = 8, and multiplying values gives f(2)·g(2) = 24; neither is composition in the stated order.

questions.prompt: If f: R → R is f(x) = 3x − 4, then f⁻¹(x) equals:

options.diagnosis: Undid the operations but kept the original sign — subtracted 4 again instead of adding it back.
Reversed each operation's sign but not their ORDER; inverting must unwind last-in-first-out.

questions.explanation: Set y = 3x − 4 and solve for x: x = (y + 4)/3, so f⁻¹(x) = (x + 4)/3. Verify: f⁻¹(f(x)) = ((3x − 4) + 4)/3 = x ✓. The reciprocal 1/f(x) fails this check completely.

questions.prompt: Consider f: R → R, f(x) = x². Which statement about its inverse is correct?

options.text: f is not invertible: it is neither one-one nor onto R
f is one-one but not onto, so it is not invertible

questions.explanation: f(2) = f(−2) = 4, so f is not one-one; and no negative number is ever an output, so f is not onto R. Failing both conditions, no inverse exists on R → R. (Restricting to f: [0,∞) → [0,∞) repairs both defects, and only then is √x the inverse.)

nodes.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
nodes.description: Sine, cosine and tangent are periodic, so they can only be inverted after restricting to principal branches: sin⁻¹ maps [−1,1] to [−π/2, π/2], cos⁻¹ to [0, π], tan⁻¹ to (−π/2, π/2). You will evaluate principal values, simplify expressions like sin⁻¹(sin x) — which is NOT always x — and use identities such as sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2. These functions are how calculators, surveyors and navigation systems recover angles from ratios, and their derivatives unlock whole families of integrals.
learning_outcomes: Can state the principal-value branches (domain and range) of sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ and tan⁻¹
Can evaluate principal values such as sin⁻¹(1/2), cos⁻¹(−1/2), tan⁻¹(−1)
Can simplify sin⁻¹(sin x) and cos⁻¹(cos x) when x lies outside the principal branch
Can apply identities like sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 and interpret graphs of inverse trig functions as reflections in y = x

misconceptions.description: Reads sin⁻¹x as the reciprocal 1/sin x (i.e. cosec x).
misconceptions.signal: Converts sin⁻¹(1/2) into 1/sin(1/2) or answers cosec values for inverse-sine questions.
misconceptions.remedy: Contrast the notations explicitly: sin⁻¹x is 'the angle whose sine is x'; the reciprocal already has its own name, cosec. Read every sin⁻¹ aloud as 'arc sine / angle whose sine is' for several sessions until the misparse dies.

misconceptions.description: Cancels blindly: sin⁻¹(sin x) = x for every x, ignoring the principal range.
misconceptions.signal: Answers 2π/3 for sin⁻¹(sin 2π/3); treats the pair as inverse machines with no restrictions.
misconceptions.remedy: Plot y = sin⁻¹(sin x) over several periods — the sawtooth shape shows the 'cancellation' only holds on [−π/2, π/2]. Teach the two-step repair: find an angle IN the principal range with the same sine (here π − 2π/3 = π/3).

misconceptions.description: Uses wrong principal ranges — e.g. returns a negative angle for cos⁻¹ of a negative number, or an angle beyond π/2 for sin⁻¹.
misconceptions.signal: States cos⁻¹(−1/2) = −π/3, or sin⁻¹(1/2) = 5π/6.
misconceptions.remedy: Anchor each branch visually on its graph slice: sin⁻¹ lives in the right half-swing [−π/2, π/2]; cos⁻¹ in the top-to-bottom sweep [0, π]. Range-check every answer against the branch chart before accepting it — cos⁻¹ NEVER outputs negatives.

real_world_hooks: Finding the angle of a ramp or ladder from its measured slope: θ = tan⁻¹(rise/run)
A surveyor recovering the elevation angle of a hilltop from distances
Robotics inverse kinematics: which joint ANGLE achieves this position?
Why your calculator's ASIN button refuses inputs beyond ±1
Satellite dish alignment: elevation angle from latitude via inverse trig

questions.prompt: The principal value of sin⁻¹(1/2) is:

options.diagnosis: Sign slip: sin(−π/6) = −1/2, not +1/2; positive inputs to sin⁻¹ give angles in (0, π/2].

questions.explanation: sin⁻¹(1/2) asks: which angle in [−π/2, π/2] has sine 1/2? That is π/6. Although sin(5π/6) = 1/2 too, 5π/6 lies outside the principal branch; and sin⁻¹ is not a reciprocal — that's cosec.

questions.prompt: The value of sin⁻¹(sin(2π/3)) is:

options.diagnosis: Knew a range correction was needed but subtracted from the wrong side (used 2π/3 − π or negated); sin(−π/3) = −√3/2 ≠ sin(2π/3).
Halved instead of reflecting; the correction is π − x, not x/2.

questions.explanation: sin(2π/3) = sin(π − 2π/3) = sin(π/3) = √3/2. Since 2π/3 lies outside [−π/2, π/2], sin⁻¹ must return the in-range angle with the same sine: sin⁻¹(√3/2) = π/3. The composition sin⁻¹(sin x) equals x only inside the principal branch.

questions.prompt: If sin⁻¹x = π/5, then cos⁻¹x equals:

options.diagnosis: Used π − π/5: applied a supplementary-angle relation where the identity is complementary (sums to π/2).
Assumed sin⁻¹ and cos⁻¹ agree at the same input; they are different angles for the same ratio.
Arithmetic slip in π/2 − π/5 = 5π/10 − 2π/10; method right, fractions wrong.

questions.explanation: For x ∈ [−1, 1], sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2. So cos⁻¹x = π/2 − π/5 = 5π/10 − 2π/10 = 3π/10. The identity reflects the complementarity sin θ = cos(π/2 − θ).

nodes.title: Matrices: Operations, Transpose, Invertibility
nodes.description: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers that adds entry-wise but multiplies by a row-into-column rule — an operation that is famously NOT commutative and defined only when inner dimensions match. You will master matrix algebra, transposes, symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices, and meet invertible matrices. Matrices encode simultaneous equations, graphics transformations, network links and the entire machinery of modern machine learning.
learning_outcomes: Can state the order of a matrix and decide when sums and products are defined
Can add, scalar-multiply and multiply matrices using the row-by-column rule
Can give examples showing AB ≠ BA and explain why matrix algebra identities differ from number algebra
Can compute transposes and classify matrices as symmetric or skew-symmetric
Can explain why AB = O does not force A = O or B = O, and recognise identity and invertible matrices

misconceptions.description: Assumes matrix multiplication is commutative: AB = BA.
misconceptions.signal: Swaps factor order freely; expands (A+B)² as A² + 2AB + B² without comment.
misconceptions.remedy: Have the student compute AB and BA for one small concrete pair and confront the different answers. Then connect to meaning: matrices are TRANSFORMATIONS, and 'rotate then reflect' visibly differs from 'reflect then rotate'.

misconceptions.description: Ports number-algebra identities wholesale: (A+B)² = A² + 2AB + B², (A+B)(A−B) = A² − B².
misconceptions.signal: Uses school identities on matrices without expanding; loses the AB + BA distinction.
misconceptions.remedy: Force the honest expansion (A+B)² = A² + AB + BA + B² and highlight that AB + BA collapses to 2AB only if the pair commutes. Verify the failure numerically with the same pair used for m1.

misconceptions.description: Multiplies matrices entry-by-entry, like addition.
misconceptions.signal: Computes (AB)ᵢⱼ = aᵢⱼ·bᵢⱼ; product of two 2×2s done in four multiplications.
misconceptions.remedy: Teach the row-into-column gesture physically (left hand sweeps a row, right hand a column, dot them). Motivate WHY via composition of linear substitutions — entry-wise product simply doesn't compute the composite.

misconceptions.description: Believes AB = O implies A = O or B = O (no zero divisors), as with numbers.
misconceptions.signal: Cancels matrices from equations: from AB = AC concludes B = C without invertibility.
misconceptions.remedy: Exhibit the classic counterexample [[0,1],[0,0]]² = O with a non-zero matrix. Frame the moral: cancellation is a PRIVILEGE purchased by invertibility, and connect forward to determinants deciding when it's granted.

real_world_hooks: Image filters: every Instagram effect is a matrix acting on pixel data
IPL points table computations as matrix operations on results
Google's PageRank: the web as a giant matrix
Cipher machines: encoding messages by matrix multiplication (Hill cipher)
Neural networks are stacks of matrix multiplications

questions.prompt: If A is a 2×3 matrix and B is a 3×4 matrix, then AB is:

options.diagnosis: Took the INNER dimensions as the answer; those must match and then cancel, leaving the outer pair.
Right dimensions, wrong order — rows of the product come from the LEFT factor.

options.text: Not defined, since A and B have different orders
options.diagnosis: Thinks multiplication needs equal orders like addition does; only the inner dimensions must agree.

questions.explanation: (2×3)·(3×4): the inner 3s match, so the product exists and has the outer dimensions 2×4. Equal orders are required for ADDITION, not multiplication.

questions.prompt: Let A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[2, 0], [1, 3]]. Then AB equals:

options.diagnosis: Row-column bookkeeping slip in the (2,1) entry: used row 2 with the wrong column entries.

questions.prompt: A and B are square matrices with AB = O (the zero matrix). Which conclusion is valid?

options.text: It is possible that neither A nor B is the zero matrix
A = O or B = O necessarily
Both A and B must be zero matrices

questions.explanation: Matrices admit zero divisors: with A = [[0,1],[0,0]] = B, AB = O though neither factor is zero. And BA need not vanish when AB does (for A = [[1,0],[0,0]], B = [[0,0],[1,0]]: AB = O but BA = [[0,0],[1,0]] ≠ O) — another casualty of non-commutativity.

nodes.title: Determinants: Properties, Adjoint, Inverse, Solving Systems
nodes.description: The determinant condenses a square matrix into a single number that decides everything: invertibility (|A| ≠ 0), the area/volume scaling of the transformation, and solvability of linear systems. You will evaluate 2×2 and 3×3 determinants by cofactor expansion, exploit row/column properties, build inverses via the adjoint A⁻¹ = adj(A)/|A|, and solve systems by the matrix method. It is the algebraic gatekeeper between unique solutions and degeneracy.
learning_outcomes: Can evaluate 2×2 and 3×3 determinants by cofactor expansion along any row or column
Can apply determinant properties: effect of row swaps, common factors, identical rows, and |kA| = kⁿ|A|
Can compute minors, cofactors and the adjoint, and find A⁻¹ = adj(A)/|A| when |A| ≠ 0
Can use determinants to test consistency and solve systems of linear equations by the matrix method
Can interpret |A| = 0 as the matrix being singular (non-invertible) and compute areas of triangles via determinants

misconceptions.description: Treats the determinant as linear over addition of matrices: |A + B| = |A| + |B|.
misconceptions.signal: Splits determinants across sums of matrices; adds determinants of parts.
misconceptions.remedy: Counterexample immediately: A = [[1,0],[0,0]], B = [[0,0],[0,1]] have |A| = |B| = 0 but |A+B| = |I| = 1. Emphasise that determinant linearity holds only ONE ROW at a time, which is a different (and correct) property.

misconceptions.description: Scales determinants wrongly: |kA| = k|A| instead of kⁿ|A| for an n×n matrix.
misconceptions.signal: For a 3×3 with |A| = 5 answers |2A| = 10.
misconceptions.remedy: Factor k out of each row one at a time, counting a factor of k per row — three rows, three factors, k³. Geometric reinforcement: doubling every edge of a box multiplies volume by 8, not 2.

misconceptions.description: Believes row operations never change a determinant — forgetting that swapping rows flips the sign and scaling a row scales the determinant.
misconceptions.signal: Freely swaps and scales rows while evaluating, reporting the wrong sign or magnitude.
misconceptions.remedy: Build a three-line 'operation ledger': swap → ×(−1); row×k → ×k; row + multiple of another → ×1. Have the student re-evaluate one determinant twice, with and without logging, to see where the sign leaked.

misconceptions.description: Forgets to divide the adjoint by the determinant (A⁻¹ = adj A, not adj A/|A|), or inverts singular matrices.
misconceptions.signal: Reports adj(A) as the inverse; never checks |A| ≠ 0 before 'inverting'.
misconceptions.remedy: Make A·A⁻¹ = I the acceptance test: multiplying A by its adjoint yields |A|·I, visibly off by the factor |A|. Precede every inversion with the ritual line '|A| = ..., ≠ 0, so A⁻¹ exists'.

real_world_hooks: Determinant as area scale factor: how a graphics transform stretches a sprite
Balancing supply-demand equations for two products: unique solution iff determinant ≠ 0
Surveyors computing a triangular plot's area straight from GPS coordinates
Cryptography: a Hill-cipher key matrix must have a nonzero determinant to decode
Structural engineering: singular stiffness matrix = unstable structure
