questions.prompt: The value of the determinant of [[3, 1], [2, 4]] is:

options.diagnosis: Added the cross products (12 + 2) instead of subtracting; the rule is ad − bc.
Subtracted in the wrong order (bc − ad); a consistent sign convention slip.
Multiplied all four entries (or the two diagonal products) together; determinant structure not yet formed.

questions.prompt: A is a 3×3 matrix with |A| = 5. The value of |2A| is:

options.diagnosis: Used k² — counted a factor of 2 for only two of the three rows.
Computed k·n·|A| = 2·3·5; blended the scaling rule with the matrix order additively.

questions.explanation: |kA| = kⁿ|A| for an n×n matrix, since k factors out of each of the n rows: |2A| = 2³ × 5 = 40. Geometrically, doubling all edges of a 3D box scales volume by 8.

questions.prompt: For A = [[4, 3], [2, 2]], the inverse A⁻¹ is:

options.diagnosis: Formed the cofactor matrix but skipped the transpose when building the adjoint.
Negated the wrong entries — swapped the sign pattern between the diagonal and off-diagonal.

questions.explanation: |A| = 4×2 − 3×2 = 2 ≠ 0, so A⁻¹ exists. For a 2×2: swap the main diagonal, negate the off-diagonal: adj A = [[2, −3], [−2, 4]], and A⁻¹ = adj A / |A| = (1/2)[[2, −3], [−2, 4]]. Check: A·A⁻¹ = I ✓ — without the 1/2 you get 2I, not I.

nodes.title: Continuity and Differentiability
nodes.description: Continuity at a point demands three things: f(a) exists, the limit exists, and they are equal — 'the pen never leaves the paper'. Differentiability is stronger: the graph must also be smooth, so |x| is continuous everywhere yet not differentiable at its corner. You will test piecewise functions, then differentiate everything in sight — composites via the chain rule, implicit relations, exponential and logarithmic functions, and parametric forms. This is the technical engine room of calculus.
learning_outcomes: Can test continuity at a point via left limit, right limit and function value, including for piecewise functions
Can determine parameter values that make a piecewise function continuous
Can explain with examples why differentiability implies continuity but not conversely (|x| at 0)
Can differentiate composite functions with the chain rule, including trig, exponential and logarithmic compositions
Can perform implicit differentiation, logarithmic differentiation and parametric differentiation, and compute second derivatives

misconceptions.description: Believes every continuous function is differentiable — smoothness comes free with unbrokenness.
misconceptions.signal: Claims |x| is differentiable at 0 'because the graph is connected'; never checks corners or cusps.
misconceptions.remedy: Zoom in on |x| at 0: a differentiable graph flattens into its tangent line under zoom, but the corner stays a corner forever. Compute the left (−1) and right (+1) difference-quotient limits to certify the failure, then bank the hierarchy: differentiable ⊂ continuous.

misconceptions.description: Reduces continuity to 'f(a) is defined' or to 'the limit exists', dropping the equality requirement.
misconceptions.signal: Declares a function continuous after checking only one of the three conditions; accepts a hole-with-dot-elsewhere graph as continuous.
misconceptions.remedy: Use a three-item checklist stamped on every problem: value ✓ limit ✓ equal ✓. Show the three distinct failure modes graphically (missing point, jump, misplaced dot) and have the student name which condition each violates.

misconceptions.description: Chain rule amputation: differentiates the outer function but forgets to multiply by the inner derivative.
misconceptions.signal: Writes d/dx sin(x²) = cos(x²); d/dx e^(3x) = e^(3x).
misconceptions.remedy: Onion-peeling protocol: name the layers u = x², y = sin u in writing, then multiply dy/du · du/dx explicitly for a dozen problems before allowing shortcuts. Numerically verify one case (slope of sin(x²) at x = 1 ≈ 1.08, not 0.54) to prove the factor is real.

misconceptions.description: Checks differentiability of a piecewise function by plugging the point into a one-sided derivative formula, never comparing both sides.
misconceptions.signal: At a boundary point computes the derivative of just one piece and declares the function differentiable; or matches function values and assumes derivatives match too.
misconceptions.remedy: Two-column ritual at every junction: left derivative | right derivative, computed separately, then compared. Reinforce with a graph where the pieces MEET (continuous) but at different slopes — visibly a kink, hence not differentiable.

real_world_hooks: Income-tax slabs: the tax function is continuous but has corners at slab boundaries
A cricket ball's bounce: position is continuous, velocity jumps — differentiability lost at impact
Electricity tariffs and cab surge pricing as piecewise functions
Zooming into a smooth curve on your phone map until it looks straight — that's differentiability
Temperature through the day: continuous, but the rate flips sign at the afternoon peak

questions.prompt: At x = 0, the function f(x) = |x| is:

options.diagnosis: Equates the corner with a break; the graph is unbroken at 0 — only smoothness fails.
Reverses the implication; differentiability ALWAYS forces continuity, so this combination is impossible for any function.

questions.explanation: lim x→0 |x| = 0 = f(0), so f is continuous. But the difference quotient has left limit −1 and right limit +1, so no single derivative exists — a corner. Continuity is necessary but not sufficient for differentiability.

questions.prompt: The derivative of sin(x²) with respect to x is:

options.diagnosis: Differentiated the inner function INSIDE the outer one; chain rule layers collapsed into each other.
Chain rule executed fully but with the sign of d(sin)/dx flipped — mixed up with the derivative of cos.

questions.explanation: Layers: y = sin u, u = x². dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx) = cos(x²) · 2x = 2x cos(x²). Omitting the inner derivative 2x is the single most common chain-rule error.

questions.prompt: f(x) = kx + 1 for x ≤ 5 and f(x) = 3x − 5 for x > 5. For what value of k is f continuous at x = 5?

options.diagnosis: Matched the SLOPES of the two pieces instead of their values; that's a (failed) differentiability condition, not continuity.
Solved 5k = 10, dropping the '+1' from the left piece while equating.
Evaluated the right piece as 3(5) + 5 = 20... or 15; substitution slip in 3x − 5 at x = 5.

questions.explanation: Continuity at 5 needs left value = right limit: 5k + 1 = 3(5) − 5 = 10, so 5k = 9 and k = 9/5. Matching coefficients of x (k = 3) would be aiming at equal slopes — a different, stronger condition that this function cannot satisfy simultaneously.

nodes.title: Applications of Derivatives: Rates, Monotonicity, Maxima and Minima
nodes.description: Derivatives go to work: related rates connect dA/dt to dr/dt through the chain rule; the sign of f′ tells where a function increases or decreases; and critical points, filtered through the first- or second-derivative test, locate maxima and minima. The crown jewels are optimisation problems — largest area, least cost, fastest route. This chapter is where calculus starts earning its keep in physics, economics and engineering.
learning_outcomes: Can solve related-rates problems by differentiating a geometric relation with respect to time
Can determine intervals of increase and decrease from the sign of f′
Can find critical points and classify them using the first- or second-derivative test
Can recognise critical points that are NOT extrema (e.g. x³ at 0) and check endpoints for absolute extrema on closed intervals
Can set up and solve optimisation word problems, verifying the nature of the optimum

misconceptions.description: Believes f′(c) = 0 guarantees a maximum or minimum at c.
misconceptions.signal: Marks every critical point as an extremum; never tests the sign change; x³ at 0 called 'a minimum'.
misconceptions.remedy: Keep x³ at 0 on permanent display: slope zero, yet the curve sails through rising on both sides. Require a verdict line for each critical point — sign chart of f′ or sign of f″ — before any max/min label is granted.

misconceptions.description: Confuses the sign of f with the sign of f′: 'f is positive here, so f is increasing here'.
misconceptions.signal: Reads increase/decrease off whether the graph is above the x-axis rather than off its slope.
misconceptions.remedy: Contrast plots: f(x) = 1/x on (0, ∞) is positive yet decreasing; f(x) = x on (−∞, 0) is negative yet increasing. Drill the sorting question 'positive or increasing?' on graph snippets until the two attributes decouple.

misconceptions.description: In related-rates problems, differentiates with respect to the space variable (or substitutes values BEFORE differentiating), missing the chain rule through time.
misconceptions.signal: From A = πr² writes dA/dt = 2πr with no dr/dt factor; plugs r = 5 into A first and differentiates a constant.
misconceptions.remedy: Enforce the sequence: relate variables symbolically → differentiate w.r.t. t (every variable earns a d/dt) → THEN substitute numbers. Annotate each term with units (cm²/s vs cm/s) so a missing dr/dt shows up as a units mismatch.

misconceptions.description: Hunts absolute extrema on a closed interval only among critical points, ignoring the endpoints.
misconceptions.signal: On [0, 3] reports the local minimum as absolute even when f(3) is larger/smaller; endpoints never evaluated.
misconceptions.remedy: Institute the candidate-list method: absolute extrema live among {critical points} ∪ {endpoints} — build the full table of values every time. A graph where the max sits at the interval's edge makes the omission visceral.

real_world_hooks: Minimising the metal in a tin can of fixed volume — real packaging economics
A ladder sliding down a wall: how fast does the top drop as the base slides?
Maximum height and range of a cricket ball or ISRO launch trajectory
Economics: marginal cost/revenue and profit maximisation where MR = MC
Air pollution balloons: rate of volume change as a balloon inflates

questions.prompt: The function f(x) = x² − 4x + 5 is increasing on:

options.diagnosis: Solved f′(x) < 0 by mistake, or flipped the inequality when isolating x; the interval found is where f DECREASES.
Solved 2x − 4 > 0 as x > 4; dropped the coefficient 2 when dividing.

questions.explanation: f′(x) = 2x − 4 > 0 ⟺ x > 2, so f increases exactly on (2, ∞). Note f(x) = (x−2)² + 1 is positive EVERYWHERE, yet it decreases until x = 2 — positivity of f and increase of f are unrelated properties.

questions.prompt: The radius of a circle is increasing at 2 cm/s. How fast is the area increasing when the radius is 5 cm?

options.diagnosis: Substituted dr/dt where r belongs: computed 2π(2) instead of 2π(5)·2; variables and rates swapped.

questions.explanation: A = πr² ⟹ dA/dt = 2πr·(dr/dt) = 2π(5)(2) = 20π cm²/s. Forgetting the dr/dt factor gives 10π (units would wrongly be cm²), and 25π is just the AREA value πr² — a quantity, not a rate.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x³, which statement about x = 0 is correct?

options.text: It is a critical point but NOT a local maximum or minimum
It is a local minimum since f′(0) = 0
It is a local maximum since f′(0) = 0
It is not a critical point since f′(0) ≠ 0
options.diagnosis: Differentiation slip: f′(x) = 3x² does vanish at 0; recompute before classifying.

questions.explanation: f′(x) = 3x² is zero at x = 0, so 0 is critical. But f′ > 0 on BOTH sides (no sign change), so f is increasing through 0 — a point of inflexion with horizontal tangent, not an extremum. f′(c) = 0 is necessary, never sufficient, for an interior extremum.

nodes.title: Integrals: Techniques and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
nodes.description: Integration reverses differentiation: an indefinite integral is a whole family of antiderivatives, differing by the constant C. You will build a toolkit — substitution, integration by parts, partial fractions, and standard forms leading to logs and inverse trig — then meet the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, which computes definite integrals as F(b) − F(a) and welds together the tangent problem and the area problem. It is arguably the single most powerful equation in mathematics.
learning_outcomes: Can find antiderivatives of standard functions and always include the constant of integration
Can integrate by substitution, recognising when an integrand contains a function and its derivative
Can integrate by parts, choosing u by the ILATE heuristic, and handle products like x·eˣ
Can evaluate definite integrals via the Fundamental Theorem as F(b) − F(a), respecting order and sign
Can use partial fractions and properties of definite integrals (e.g. ∫₀ᵃ f(x)dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a−x)dx) to simplify evaluation

misconceptions.description: Drops the constant of integration — believes d/dx and ∫ cancel exactly, so each function has ONE antiderivative.
misconceptions.signal: Writes ∫x² dx = x³/3; loses solution families in differential equations later.
misconceptions.remedy: Differentiate x³/3, x³/3 + 7 and x³/3 − 42 and watch all three collapse to x²: the reverse journey cannot know which one you left from. Graph the family as parallel curves; make a missing +C cost a mark ritually.

misconceptions.description: Integrates products factor-by-factor: ∫f·g dx = (∫f dx)(∫g dx).
misconceptions.signal: Writes ∫x eˣ dx = (x²/2)eˣ; never reaches for parts or substitution.
misconceptions.remedy: Differentiate the claimed answer and watch the product rule spray extra terms — it cannot reproduce the integrand. Mirror the lesson from differentiation: products need their own machinery (integration by parts), which is the product rule run backwards.

misconceptions.description: Reverses direction: differentiates instead of anti-differentiating (∫x² dx = 2x), or applies the power rule with the exponent going down.
misconceptions.signal: Power drops by one under an integral sign; ∫cos x dx = −sin x (differentiated instead).
misconceptions.remedy: Institute the verification loop: every integral answer must be differentiated back to the integrand before submission. The habit is self-correcting — 2x differentiates to 2, not x², and the error surfaces immediately.

misconceptions.description: Mishandles the Fundamental Theorem: computes F(a) − F(b), adds F(b) + F(a), or appends +C to definite integrals.
misconceptions.signal: Definite integral answers off by sign, or doubled; writes '7 + C' for a definite integral.
misconceptions.remedy: Verbalise F(b) − F(a) as 'net change from a to b — end minus start', like a trip odometer. Show the constant cancelling: (F(b)+C) − (F(a)+C) kills C, so definite integrals are numbers, not families.

real_world_hooks: Odometer from speedometer: integrating speed over time recovers distance
Total rainfall from a rain-intensity graph during a monsoon downpour
ISRO: integrating thrust acceleration to get a rocket's velocity profile
Electricity bill: energy = integral of power drawn over the month
Area of an irregular plot of farmland as an integral

questions.prompt: ∫x² dx equals:

options.diagnosis: Raised the power but forgot to divide by the new exponent; differentiate back to see 3x², not x².

questions.explanation: The power rule for integration raises the exponent and divides by it: ∫x² dx = x³/3 + C. The +C is essential — every function of the form x³/3 + constant has derivative x². Always check by differentiating.

questions.prompt: Evaluate ∫₁² 3x² dx.

options.diagnosis: Antiderivative taken as 3x³ — forgot to divide by the new exponent (3x³/3 = x³); then 24 − 3 = 21.

questions.explanation: ∫3x² dx = x³, so the definite integral is [x³]₁² = 2³ − 1³ = 8 − 1 = 7. It is end-value MINUS start-value: forgetting to subtract F(1) gives 8; adding gives 9.

questions.prompt: ∫x eˣ dx equals:

options.diagnosis: Sign slip inside integration by parts: added ∫eˣ dx instead of subtracting it.
Treated eˣ as if it absorbs the integral unchanged and x as a passive constant; parts never applied.

questions.explanation: By parts with u = x, dv = eˣdx: ∫x eˣ dx = x eˣ − ∫eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ + C = (x − 1)eˣ + C. Verify by differentiating: (x − 1)eˣ + eˣ = x eˣ ✓. Integrating the factors separately — (x²/2)(eˣ) — fails this check.

nodes.title: Applications of Integrals: Areas Under Curves
nodes.description: The definite integral becomes a measuring tool: the area under a curve is ∫y dx, the area between two curves is the integral of (upper − lower), and regions bounded by parabolas, circles and lines yield to careful setup. The crucial subtlety is that a raw definite integral counts area below the x-axis as negative — geometric area requires splitting at the crossings and taking absolute values. Sketch first, integrate second.
learning_outcomes: Can sketch the region described by curves and lines before setting up any integral
Can compute the area under a curve between two ordinates using a definite integral
Can split an integral at x-axis crossings and combine absolute values to get true geometric area
Can compute the area between two curves by integrating (upper − lower) between intersection points found algebraically

misconceptions.description: Discards or mangles regions below the x-axis: reports a negative 'area' or silently drops the negative lobe.
misconceptions.signal: States an area as −2; for sin x on [0, 2π] computes only the first arch and answers 2.
misconceptions.remedy: Shade both lobes of sin x on [0, 2π] in different colours and ask 'is the lower pool of paint less real?'. Establish the protocol: find the crossings, integrate each piece, add |values| — and that any final negative area means a setup error.

misconceptions.description: Equates the plain definite integral with geometric area even when the curve crosses the axis: ∫₀²π sin x dx = 0, 'so the area is 0'.
misconceptions.signal: Reports 0 area for visibly shaded regions; never splits the interval at roots of the function.
misconceptions.remedy: Distinguish the two questions explicitly — NET signed accumulation vs PAINT needed. Compute both for the same curve and tabulate them side by side so the student owns both concepts rather than merging them.

misconceptions.description: Integrates (f − g) between curves without establishing which is on top (or without finding intersections), yielding sign errors or wrong limits.
misconceptions.signal: Gets a negative between-curves area and just flips the sign at the end without understanding; uses guessed limits.
misconceptions.remedy: Make the sketch non-negotiable: mark intersection points by solving f = g, test one x between them to crown the upper curve, then write ∫(upper − lower). The 'test a point' step converts guessing into verification.

real_world_hooks: Land area of a river-bounded field: the boundary is a curve, the survey is an integral
Cricket wagon wheels and Manhattan charts: area under a run-rate curve is total runs
Cross-sectional area of a dam or road embankment from its design curves
Work from a force-displacement graph in physics is literally area under the curve
Velocity-time graphs: area above vs below the axis = forward vs backward displacement

questions.prompt: The area under the line y = 2x, above the x-axis, from x = 0 to x = 3 is:

options.diagnosis: Multiplied base by height (3 × 6) as if the region were a rectangle; the region is a triangle — the integral supplies the missing 1/2 automatically.
Applied an extra factor of 1/2 to the already-correct integral; double-counted the triangle formula on top of ∫2x dx.
Evaluated y(3) = 6 — reported the height of the region, not its area.

questions.explanation: Area = ∫₀³ 2x dx = [x²]₀³ = 9. Geometric check: the region is a right triangle with base 3 and height 6, area = ½ × 3 × 6 = 9 ✓. The integral IS the triangle formula here — don't apply ½ twice.

questions.prompt: The total area enclosed between y = sin x and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2π is:

options.diagnosis: Reported the length of the interval; area needs the integral of the function, not the width of the window.

questions.explanation: ∫₀^π sin x dx = 2 (upper arch) and ∫_π^{2π} sin x dx = −2 (lower arch). The signed total is 0, but geometric area = |2| + |−2| = 4. Splitting at the crossing x = π is what separates 'net accumulation' from 'area'.

questions.prompt: The area of the region enclosed between the curves y = x² and y = x is:

options.diagnosis: Added the two individual integrals (1/2 + 1/3) instead of subtracting lower from upper.
Integrated only one curve (x²) over [0,1]; the enclosed region needs the difference of the two.

questions.explanation: Intersections: x² = x at x = 0, 1. On (0, 1), the line y = x is above y = x² (test x = ½: 0.5 > 0.25). Area = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = [x²/2 − x³/3]₀¹ = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6. Integrating (x² − x) instead gives −1/6 — the sign says 'you subtracted upper from lower'.

nodes.title: Differential Equations: Separable and First-order Linear
nodes.description: A differential equation relates a function to its derivatives — it describes how something changes and asks you to recover the thing itself. You will read off order and degree, solve separable equations by gathering each variable to its own side, and solve first-order linear equations dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x) with the integrating factor e^∫P dx. General solutions carry arbitrary constants; initial conditions pin down particular solutions. This is the native language of physics, biology and economics: growth, decay, cooling, circuits, epidemics.
learning_outcomes: Can determine the order and degree (when defined) of a differential equation
Can verify that a given function is a solution of a differential equation
Can solve separable equations, keeping the arbitrary constant and simplifying it legitimately
Can solve dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x) using the integrating factor e^∫P dx
Can apply initial conditions to extract particular solutions and model growth/decay situations

misconceptions.description: Confuses order with degree: order is the highest derivative present; degree is the power of that highest derivative (in polynomial form).
misconceptions.signal: For (d²y/dx²)³ + (dy/dx)⁴ = 0 answers 'order 3' or 'degree 2'; swaps the two labels under pressure.
misconceptions.remedy: Two-question drill on many examples: 'How DEEP does differentiation go?' (order) then 'What POWER sits on that deepest derivative?' (degree). Flag the trap that other, lower derivatives' powers (like the 4 here) are pure distractors.

misconceptions.description: Mishandles arbitrary constants: drops C entirely, adds a separate C to both sides and cancels them, or expects the count of constants to equal the degree instead of the order.
misconceptions.signal: Presents y = x as 'the' solution of dy/dx = y/x; writes ln y + C = ln x + C ⟹ y = x.
misconceptions.remedy: Show the one-parameter family y = Cx as a fan of lines all satisfying the equation, so losing C visibly loses almost every solution. Rule: integrate both sides, write ONE constant on one side immediately, and rename combined constants honestly (C₂ − C₁ = C).

misconceptions.description: Bungles the integrating factor: uses ∫P dx itself (without exponentiating), or e^P without integrating.
misconceptions.signal: For dy/dx + (2/x)y = x writes IF = 2 ln x or e^(2/x) instead of e^(2 ln x) = x².
misconceptions.remedy: Drill the three-step chant 'integrate P → exponentiate → multiply through', writing each artifact separately. Verify the factor works: after multiplying, the left side must collapse to d/dx(IF·y) — if it doesn't, the factor is wrong.

misconceptions.description: Separates variables illegally: moves terms additively across dy/dx, or divides by expressions that could be zero without noting lost solutions.
misconceptions.signal: From dy/dx = x + y writes dy = x dx + y... then integrates; loses y = 0 solutions when dividing by y.
misconceptions.remedy: Test separability first: can the RHS be written as f(x)·g(y)? (x + y cannot.) When dividing by g(y), park the case g(y) = 0 in a margin note and check at the end whether constant solutions were lost.

real_world_hooks: Chai cooling on the table follows Newton's law of cooling — a separable equation
Population growth of a city and compound interest are dy/dt = ky in disguise
Carbon dating an archaeological find from its decay equation
Epidemic spread curves (as seen during COVID) come from differential equations
A parachutist's terminal velocity: solving dv/dt = g − kv

questions.prompt: The order and degree of the differential equation (d²y/dx²)³ + (dy/dx)⁴ + y = 0 are:

options.diagnosis: Took the highest power appearing ANYWHERE; degree reads the power of the HIGHEST-ORDER derivative only.
Read the order off the largest exponent (4) rather than the deepest derivative (second).

questions.explanation: The highest derivative present is d²y/dx² → order 2. Its power (with the equation polynomial in derivatives) is 3 → degree 3. The exponent 4 on the FIRST derivative is a deliberate distractor — degree only looks at the highest-order derivative.

questions.prompt: The general solution of dy/dx = y/x (x, y > 0) is:

options.diagnosis: Integrated the x-side as if the equation were dy = (1/x)... treated y on the right as a constant instead of separating dy/y = dx/x.

questions.explanation: Separate: dy/y = dx/x. Integrate: ln y = ln x + C₁, so y = e^{C₁}x = Cx — a one-parameter family of lines through the origin. Cancelling the constants to get y = x keeps only ONE member of the family; a sign slip (dy/y = −dx/x) would give the hyperbolas xy = C instead.

questions.prompt: The integrating factor of the differential equation dy/dx + (2/x)y = x (x > 0) is:

options.diagnosis: Integrated 2/x as 2x — power-rule slip on 1/x, whose integral is ln x, not x²/2 scaled.

questions.explanation: P(x) = 2/x, so ∫P dx = 2 ln x, and IF = e^{2 ln x} = e^{ln x²} = x². Check: multiplying through by x² gives x²y′ + 2xy = x³, whose left side is exactly d/dx(x²y) ✓ — the collapse test every integrating factor must pass.

nodes.title: Vector Algebra: Dot and Cross Products
nodes.description: Vectors carry magnitude and direction, and two different 'multiplications' extract different geometry: the dot product a·b = |a||b|cos θ is a SCALAR measuring alignment (zero means perpendicular), while the cross product a×b is a VECTOR perpendicular to both, with magnitude |a||b|sin θ equal to the parallelogram's area (zero means parallel). You will compute both in component form, find projections, angles, areas and unit normals. This is the working mathematics of forces, torques and 3D graphics.
learning_outcomes: Can represent vectors in component form, compute magnitudes, unit vectors and section-formula combinations
Can compute dot products, use them to find angles and projections, and characterise perpendicularity by a·b = 0
Can compute cross products via the determinant rule, use |a×b| for areas, and characterise parallelism by a×b = 0
Can state which product yields a scalar and which a vector, and that a×b = −(b×a) while a·b = b·a

misconceptions.description: Adds magnitudes when adding vectors: |a + b| = |a| + |b| regardless of directions.
misconceptions.signal: Claims two forces of 3 N and 4 N always total 7 N; triangle inequality never mentioned.
misconceptions.remedy: Walk the displacement: 3 km east then 4 km north lands you 5 km away, not 7. Let the student drag two arrows in an applet through angles 0° to 180° and watch |a+b| slide between 7 and 1 — equality only when perfectly aligned.

misconceptions.description: Confuses the output TYPES of the two products: expects a·b to be a vector, or a×b to be a number.
misconceptions.signal: Writes a·b with i, j, k components; reports |a×b| when the vector a×b is asked, or vice versa.
misconceptions.remedy: Attach each product to its geometric deliverable: dot = 'how much alignment?' (one number), cross = 'the axis perpendicular to both, sized by area' (an arrow). Type-check every equation: a scalar can never equal a vector, so errors become syntax errors.

misconceptions.description: From a·b = 0 concludes a = 0 or b = 0, missing perpendicularity (and symmetrically for a×b = 0 missing parallelism).
misconceptions.signal: Treats zero products like zero products of numbers; surprised that i·j = 0 for two 'perfectly good' vectors.
misconceptions.remedy: Make i·j = 0 and i×i = 0 canonical examples: nonzero vectors with vanishing products. Reframe zero as INFORMATION — dot zero says 'perpendicular', cross zero says 'parallel' — rather than as degeneracy.

misconceptions.description: Treats the cross product as commutative: a×b = b×a.
misconceptions.signal: Swaps factors freely in cross products; sign of the normal vector comes out random.
misconceptions.remedy: Right-hand rule physically, both orders: curling from a to b points the thumb opposite to curling from b to a, so a×b = −(b×a). Contrast in the same breath with the dot product, which IS symmetric, to prevent overcorrection.

real_world_hooks: Work done = force · displacement (dot); torque on a spanner = r × F (cross)
A boat crossing a river: velocity vectors add tip-to-tail, not magnitude-to-magnitude
Cricket fielding: the throw to the keeper as a 3D displacement vector
Game engines light surfaces using the normal vector from a cross product
ISRO thrust vectoring: resolving engine force along and across the flight path (projection)

questions.prompt: If a = 2i + 3j − k and b = i − j + 2k, then a·b equals:

options.diagnosis: Sign slip on the k-term: (−1)(2) taken as +2; components multiplied right, one sign lost.
Took absolute values of the component products (2 + 3 − 2 → all positive); signs of components ignored.

questions.explanation: a·b = (2)(1) + (3)(−1) + (−1)(2) = 2 − 3 − 2 = −3. The dot product is a SCALAR — a single signed number measuring alignment — never a vector of component products.

questions.prompt: a and b are NON-ZERO vectors with a·b = 0. What must be true?

options.text: At least one of a, b is the zero vector

options.diagnosis: Swapped the zero conditions of the two products: it is a×b = 0 that signals parallel vectors.
Assumes all products vanish together; for perpendicular vectors the cross product is at its LARGEST (|a||b|).

questions.explanation: a·b = |a||b|cos θ = 0 with both magnitudes nonzero forces cos θ = 0, i.e. θ = 90°. Perpendicular nonzero vectors (like i and j) have zero dot product — and simultaneously the maximal cross product, since sin 90° = 1.

questions.prompt: For a = i + j and b = i − j, the cross product a × b equals:
questions.explanation: a × b = det[[i, j, k], [1, 1, 0], [1, −1, 0]] = i(1·0 − 0·(−1)) − j(1·0 − 0·1) + k(1·(−1) − 1·1) = −2k. Computing b × a instead gives +2k (anticommutativity), and the answer must be a VECTOR along k, not the bare number −2.

nodes.title: Three-Dimensional Geometry: Lines and Planes
nodes.description: Vectors turn spatial geometry into computation: a line is r = a + λb (a point plus a direction), specified by direction ratios or the normalized direction cosines with l² + m² + n² = 1. You will find angles between lines using their direction vectors, the shortest distance between skew lines, and work with planes through their normal vectors — including the distance from a point to a plane. This is the geometry of flight paths, laser alignment and 3D modelling.
learning_outcomes: Can convert direction ratios to direction cosines by dividing by the magnitude, and verify l² + m² + n² = 1
Can write vector and Cartesian equations of a line through a point with a given direction, or through two points
Can compute the angle between two lines from their direction vectors and test parallel/perpendicular conditions
Can find the shortest distance between skew lines and the distance from a point to a plane
Can relate the angle between a line and a plane to the angle with the plane's normal (complementary angles)

misconceptions.description: Uses direction ratios directly as direction cosines, skipping normalisation by the magnitude.
misconceptions.signal: States the direction cosines of ratios 2, −1, 2 as (2, −1, 2); l² + m² + n² comes out as 9 and no alarm rings.
misconceptions.remedy: Install the checksum: direction cosines MUST satisfy l² + m² + n² = 1 — have the student verify it on every answer. Connect cosines to meaning: they are literal cosines of angles with the axes, so none can exceed 1 in magnitude.

misconceptions.description: Confuses the angle a line makes with a plane with the angle it makes with the plane's NORMAL (they are complements).
misconceptions.signal: Uses cos θ = |b·n|/(|b||n|) for a line-plane angle without converting; answers off by exactly 90° − θ.
misconceptions.remedy: Draw the side-view triangle: line, its shadow in the plane, and the normal — the line-plane angle sits between line and shadow, and line-normal is its complement. Anchor the formula sin θ = |b·n|/(|b||n|) to that picture rather than to memory.

misconceptions.description: Garbles parallel/perpendicular tests: e.g. declares planes parallel when their normals are perpendicular, or lines perpendicular when direction ratios are proportional.
misconceptions.signal: Applies a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂ = 0 as a parallelism test; mixes up proportionality vs zero dot product.
misconceptions.remedy: Route every test through the carrier vectors: planes inherit behaviour from their NORMALS, lines from their DIRECTIONS. Parallel ⟺ vectors proportional; perpendicular ⟺ dot product zero. Two worked contrasts side by side lock the mapping.

misconceptions.description: Computes point-to-plane distance without dividing by |n|: uses |ax₁ + by₁ + cz₁ + d| alone.
misconceptions.signal: Distances come out |n| times too large; answer changes if the plane equation is scaled by 2, and the student doesn't notice the inconsistency.
misconceptions.remedy: Expose the scale bug: 6x − 3y + 2z = 4 and 12x − 6y + 4z = 8 are the SAME plane but give different unnormalised 'distances'. Dividing by |n| restores invariance — tie to the unit-normal form of the plane equation.

real_world_hooks: Two flight paths over an airport: skew lines and their minimum separation (air-safety distance)
A mobile tower's guy-wires: angles between cables and the ground plane
Laser levelling on a construction site: point-to-plane distances
Drone waypoint navigation: lines in space via point + direction
Docking at the ISS: aligning a spacecraft's approach line with the docking plane's normal

questions.prompt: The direction cosines of a line with direction ratios 2, −1, 2 are:

options.diagnosis: Divided by the SQUARED magnitude (4+1+4 = 9) instead of its square root 3.
Divided by the sum of absolute values (2+1+2 = 5) instead of √(sum of squares).

questions.explanation: Magnitude = √(2² + (−1)² + 2²) = √9 = 3, so (l, m, n) = (2/3, −1/3, 2/3). Checksum: (2/3)² + (1/3)² + (2/3)² = 9/9 = 1 ✓ — direction cosines must always pass this test.

questions.prompt: The distance of the point (2, 5, −3) from the plane 6x − 3y + 2z − 4 = 0 is:

options.diagnosis: Divided by |n|² = 49 rather than |n| = 7; normalised twice.
Sign slip on the z-term: 2(−3) taken as +6, giving |12 − 15 + 6 − 4| = 1 in the numerator.

questions.explanation: d = |6(2) − 3(5) + 2(−3) − 4| / √(6² + 3² + 2²) = |12 − 15 − 6 − 4| / √49 = 13/7. The division by |n| = 7 is what makes the answer independent of how the plane equation is scaled.

questions.prompt: A line makes an angle of 30° with a plane. The angle between the line and the plane's normal is:

options.diagnosis: Took the supplement (180° − 30°) instead of the complement; the normal stands at 90° to the plane, not 180°.
Believes a line is always perpendicular to a plane's normal — that holds only for lines LYING IN the plane.

questions.explanation: The normal is perpendicular to the plane, so (line, normal) + (line, plane) = 90°. With the plane angle 30°, the normal angle is 60°. This is why the line-plane formula uses sin θ where the line-line formula uses cos θ.

nodes.title: Linear Programming
nodes.description: Linear programming optimises a linear objective Z = ax + by subject to linear constraints: graph the inequalities, intersect them into a feasible region, and use the corner-point theorem — the optimum, if it exists, occurs at a vertex. Unbounded regions demand one extra check before declaring victory. Born from wartime logistics, LP now schedules airlines, blends diets, allocates factory time and routes deliveries.
learning_outcomes: Can translate a word problem into decision variables, a linear objective function and linear constraints
Can graph the constraints and identify the feasible region, including non-negativity restrictions
Can apply the corner-point method: find vertices, evaluate Z at each, and select the optimum
Can handle unbounded regions correctly, checking whether the candidate optimum is genuine via the open half-plane test

misconceptions.description: Believes the optimum can sit anywhere in the feasible region (or at its 'centre'), so tests arbitrary interior points.
misconceptions.signal: Evaluates Z at a scatter of interior points and picks the best; never enumerates vertices.
misconceptions.remedy: Slide the objective line Z = c interactively across the region: it exits the region at a corner (or an entire edge), never at an interior point. Level-line intuition makes the corner-point theorem feel inevitable instead of arbitrary.

misconceptions.description: Evaluates the objective at intersection points that are NOT in the feasible region (constraint lines crossing outside it).
misconceptions.signal: Vertex list includes points violating some constraint; 'optimal' point fails substitution into the constraints.
misconceptions.remedy: Add a verification column to the vertex table: every candidate must satisfy ALL constraints before Z is computed. Shade the infeasible side of each line in grey so illegal intersections are visually dead on arrival.

misconceptions.description: Mishandles unbounded regions: either declares 'no optimum ever exists', or blindly trusts the corner-point value without the half-plane check.
misconceptions.signal: Refuses to minimise over an unbounded region; or reports a 'maximum' that the region actually exceeds beyond every bound.
misconceptions.remedy: Work one example each way: a minimum that DOES exist on an unbounded region, and a maximum that doesn't. Teach the decisive test: after finding candidate value M, check whether the open half-plane (Z beyond M) intersects the region — empty means M is genuine.

misconceptions.description: Shades the wrong side of a constraint line, or forgets the non-negativity constraints x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
misconceptions.signal: Feasible regions extend into negative quadrants; region on the wrong side of ≤ lines.
misconceptions.remedy: Test-point ritual: substitute (0,0) (or another off-line point) into every inequality and shade the side that passes. Physically box the first quadrant first whenever x, y ≥ 0 appear — production quantities can't be negative.

real_world_hooks: A tailor with limited cloth and stitching hours maximising profit on shirts vs kurtas
Diet problems: cheapest thali meeting protein and calorie requirements
Airline crew and train timetable scheduling are industrial-scale LPs
A dabbawala-style delivery fleet minimising cost under route constraints
Farm planning: allocating acres between two crops under water and labour limits

questions.prompt: In a linear programming problem with a bounded feasible region, the maximum of the objective function Z occurs:

options.text: At a corner point (vertex) of the feasible region
At the centre of the feasible region
At any interior point where Z is large
At the feasible point farthest from the origin
options.diagnosis: Conflates the objective function with distance; for Z = x − 2y, points NEAR the origin can beat far ones.

questions.explanation: The corner-point theorem: on a bounded feasible region, a linear objective attains its maximum and minimum at vertices (possibly along a whole edge, but always including a vertex). Level lines of Z sweep across the region and last touch it at a corner.

questions.prompt: The corner points of a feasible region are (0,0), (4,0), (0,5) and (2,4). The maximum of Z = 3x + 4y is:

options.diagnosis: Evaluated only the axis vertices (4,0) and (0,5); the mixed vertex (2,4) was skipped.
Maximised 3x alone using (4,0); the y-term's contribution to Z was ignored.

questions.explanation: Z(0,0) = 0; Z(4,0) = 12; Z(0,5) = 20; Z(2,4) = 6 + 16 = 22. The maximum is 22 at (2,4). Every listed vertex must be evaluated — and only listed (feasible) vertices count; a point like (4,3) giving 24 lies outside the region.

questions.prompt: A feasible region is UNBOUNDED and the smallest value of Z = x + 2y over its corner points is 6. When is 6 actually the minimum of Z?

options.text: When the open half-plane x + 2y < 6 has no point in common with the feasible region
Never — an unbounded region cannot have a minimum
Always — the smallest corner value is automatically the minimum
Only if the region also contains the origin

questions.explanation: On unbounded regions the corner-point method needs a final check: draw x + 2y < 6. If that open half-plane misses the region entirely, no feasible point beats 6, so 6 is the true minimum; if it intersects the region, Z dips below 6 and no minimum exists at the corners. Unboundedness threatens maxima and minima differently — each case needs this test, not a blanket rule.

nodes.title: Probability: Conditional Probability, Bayes' Theorem, Random Variables
nodes.description: Probability learns from information: P(A|B) re-weights chances given that B occurred, the multiplication rule chains events, and independence means P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B). Bayes' theorem reverses conditionals — from P(evidence|cause) to P(cause|evidence) — the logic behind medical testing and spam filters, where base rates routinely humiliate intuition. Random variables then attach numbers to outcomes, with probability distributions and means (expected values) to summarise them.
learning_outcomes: Can compute conditional probabilities from the definition P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) and from two-way tables
Can apply the multiplication rule and test events for independence via P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B)
Can distinguish independent events from mutually exclusive events with examples
Can apply the total probability theorem and Bayes' theorem to reverse conditional probabilities
Can construct the probability distribution of a discrete random variable and compute its mean (expected value)

misconceptions.description: Swaps the conditional: treats P(A|B) as equal to P(B|A).
misconceptions.signal: Reports a test's accuracy P(positive|disease) as the answer to 'given a positive, what's the chance of disease?'.
misconceptions.remedy: Contrast the two with a stark verbal pair: P(rain | monsoon month) vs P(monsoon month | rain). Then run one Bayes computation with concrete counts (a 10,000-person table) so the student SEES the two conditionals come out wildly different.

misconceptions.description: Equates independence with mutual exclusivity: 'independent events can't happen together'.
misconceptions.signal: Sets P(A∩B) = 0 for independent events; claims disjoint events are independent 'because they don't affect each other'.
misconceptions.remedy: Flip it: mutually exclusive events are MAXIMALLY dependent — knowing A happened tells you B certainly didn't. Verify with numbers: P(A)P(B) > 0 ≠ 0 = P(A∩B) for disjoint events with positive probabilities. Independence means information about one leaves the other's probability UNCHANGED.

misconceptions.description: Multiplies unconditionally: P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) even for dependent events (e.g. drawing without replacement).
misconceptions.signal: Two aces without replacement computed as (4/52)², not (4/52)(3/51).
misconceptions.remedy: Slow-motion the second draw: the deck now has 51 cards and 3 aces — the sample space itself changed. Make the general rule primary — P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B|A) — with plain multiplication as the special case earned only by verified independence.

misconceptions.description: Base-rate neglect: ignores the prior in Bayes problems, so a 90%-accurate test 'means' 90% chance of disease after a positive.
misconceptions.signal: Answers near the test's accuracy regardless of how rare the condition is; shocked by the true answer.
misconceptions.remedy: Natural frequencies beat formulas: of 10,000 people, 100 have the disease → 90 true positives; of 9,900 healthy → 990 false positives. Only 90 of the 1,080 positives are real (~8%). Build the tree BEFORE the formula, every time.

real_world_hooks: Medical screening: why a positive result for a rare disease is less scary than it sounds
Spam filters: Bayes' theorem deciding if 'lottery winner!' mail is junk
Cricket: probability a batsman scores 50+ GIVEN the team batted first (conditional from data tables)
Insurance and expected value: how premiums are priced
Weather app 'chance of rain' updating as new radar evidence arrives

questions.prompt: Given P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A∩B) = 0.2, find P(A|B).

options.diagnosis: Computed P(A∪B) = 0.6 + 0.5 − 0.2; union and conditional formulas interchanged.

questions.explanation: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) = 0.2/0.5 = 0.4 — condition on B by dividing by B's probability. Dividing by P(A) instead gives P(B|A) = 0.2/0.6 = 1/3, a different question; and 0.3 = P(A)P(B) wrongly presumes independence.

questions.prompt: A and B are INDEPENDENT events with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4. Then P(A∩B) is:

options.diagnosis: Applied the addition rule to an 'and' question; union and intersection swapped.
Computed P(A∪B) = 0.3 + 0.4 − 0.12 — right machinery, but answered the union instead of the intersection.

questions.explanation: For independent events, P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12. Independence does NOT mean the events can't co-occur — that's mutual exclusivity, and disjoint events with positive probabilities are never independent.

questions.prompt: A disease affects 1% of a population. A test detects it with probability 0.9 in the diseased, but also gives a false positive with probability 0.1 in the healthy. If a random person tests positive, the probability they actually have the disease is:

options.diagnosis: Computed the numerator P(disease ∩ positive) but never divided by the total probability of testing positive.
Reported the prior unchanged — the positive test result was given no evidential weight at all.

questions.explanation: Bayes: P(D|+) = (0.01×0.9) / (0.01×0.9 + 0.99×0.1) = 0.009/0.108 = 1/12 ≈ 8.3%. In a town of 10,000: 90 true positives vs 990 false positives — only 90 of 1,080 positives are real. The rarity of the disease (base rate) drags the answer far below the test's 90% accuracy.
